Proc. fol. 1795v.: From Abbot Tosti of Foligno I heard that Freemasonry had singled out our Sisters in that city, and that one night, the Servant of God being in our house, fire was set to the great door, and that the Servant of God, having heard the noise, looked out, saw the flames and a man with a knife in his hand. Despising the danger, she went down with her Sisters and crossed the flames, followed by them. This fact is known to the whole Institute. On the occasion of the explosion of the powder magazine in 1895, I think, we were all terrified, and we ran to the Servant of God, who was not calm only for herself, but knew how to instill calm in us too.

§ 529
A lively character, but always mistress of herself.

She also despised the risks on the occasion of epidemic diseases, and leprosy she caught precisely because of this contempt of hers. She had, in short, no measure in giving of herself, caring not at all about dangers.

As to natural character, one saw that the Servant of God must have been very sensitive and lively; but she had made herself master of it so as not to let herself be overcome by her liveliness in any circumstance, however provoking, as I verified many times. Sometimes I saw her indignant, angry never.

Her firmness was her finest side, for she seemed an unshakable rock, on which she founded the Institute. If she did not see in it the glory of God, one could make requests of her either as a favor or with insistence, it was useless, she did not budge.

The Servant of God knew no intemperance of any kind. In food she was sparing in an unbelievable way.

§ 530
Temperance and mortification.

In Holy Week, on Thursday and Friday she took no food at all. She shut herself in her room and did not leave it except to attend the services. She fasted on the eve of the Immaculate Conception and the last days of carnival in a way that made us pity her. At indeterminate but frequent times she returned to fast strictly. On these days Sr. A. Borromea brought her the soup, and she tasted a few spoonfuls and left the rest; so when she brought her the first dish of vegetables, two forkfuls, and that was all; and so with the other dish. She said, to hide her fast, that she felt a little unwell. She was, however, unaffected in these fasts and tried not to let them show. We observed sometimes that of the roll, of which half always remained for her, the other half, breaking it, she had made disappear with the cutlery on the plates that were taken back to the kitchen.

§ 531
Poverty.

Proc. fol. 1805: Poverty. The Servant of God dressed altogether like us, not only in form but also in the quality of the cloth, and it was admirable how she observed the smallest particulars, she wanted us too to conform perfectly. Sometimes the novice mistress brought us a scapular of the Mother, which we, out of devotion, divided among ourselves; but we noticed at the same time that it had turned green and worn. The same mistress then told us that the Mother had not stripped herself of that scapular, but that the Sisters had taken it from her.

In her room one saw that for her own use she had only the bare necessary. Her bed, which is still preserved in her little room in this house, was very simple; she never used sheets, except in case of illness. Two chairs, the coarsest in the house, a little table that served as her desk, two lamps, one for work and the other with Mira night-lights for the night, a large Crucifix, a built-in cupboard, made up the furnishing of her room, and I remember nothing else.

Once I was present when the wardrobe keeper came to tell the Servant of God that her personal linen could no longer be mended.

§ 532
Community poverty.

She required of her daughters the observance of poverty, and woe if any, for a sore throat, put on a silk handkerchief, or wore it in sight: she allowed it but hidden. And once, when she was ill with her throat, great pains had to be taken to make her accept a silk handkerchief; she preferred cotton, saying that this is the silk of the poor.

In her exhortations she insisted much on the observance of the vow of poverty, going down practically to the smallest particulars; as for example: the use of an armchair or one with a higher back was not for the poor. And she used the chair as if it were a stool, that is, without leaning on the back.

She recommended to the Superiors the observance of poverty, but wanted at the same time that when the Sisters went about they should not have patches too visible on the habit.

She presented to us the virtue of obedience in such a way as to make us absolutely fall in love with that vow.

§ 533
Doctrine and practice of obedience.

«As air is indispensable to you for living, — she said to us —, so obedience is for the religious life». «A religious without obedience is like a shadow walking about the Cloister without belonging to it».

Once, on St. Anne's day, after giving others a thought, she gave one also to me, saying: «You will have to go to paradise by the virtue of obedience. Until now you have scraped along with this virtue; but you will have to exercise it perfectly with its qualities; for obedience must be blind, prompt and slave». And as I played the terrified one at this last word, she explained to me how such slavery is that which gives the widest freedom. «You will understand better afterward, — she added —, and you will be able to tell me».

She instructed the Superiors on the manner of giving obedience. She wanted them to adapt to characters, and not to use very grave words, such as «under precept of obedience» for very light things, «because, — she said —, it would generate confusion in timid and scrupulous souls between the substance of obedience and the form».

She, moreover, was so deferential in conversation to what others said, to customs, to counsels, that nothing more could be desired.

Although she had (I believe) no faith in medicines, she gave heed and obeyed when told to take them.

§ 534
Vigilance and practice of chastity.

As to Chastity, she wanted the religious to use expressions, both in teaching and in speaking with doctors, the most modest and reserved, without however departing from the meaning. For example, in place of sensuality, they should use physical sense, and the like.

She sought to raise the more timid sisters, to whom attending operations that our rules permitted made an impression, to a supernatural reason, so that they should look at everything in Jesus and for love of him. And for her own part she was so reserved that we Sisters never succeeded in seeing that she had her sleeves above the wrist.

I never succeeded in obtaining leave to enter her room.

The doctor never succeeded in more than taking her pulse. Her nurses told me that the Mother never had need of anyone, even to undress and dress, and that she never had herself rendered any service, not even of those that the most reserved and purest persons do not refuse, believing she was not failing in the fair virtue.

§ 535
Humility, the characteristic virtue of the Servant of God.

Proc. fol. 1819v.: If the Servant of God was great in the exercise of the other virtues, she excelled above all in the practice of humility. She wished that her person should disappear as much as possible. On the occasion of the exhibition of sacred art at Turin, to a Sister who asked her how to behave before the Royals who would attend, she answered: «Do you ask me these things? I really know nothing: I have never dealt with the great». In this connection it comes to my mind that once she had to present herself to the Duchess of Genoa and was obliged to have recourse to friends who gave her suitable dresses, she being without them. This fact I heard told many times by our Sisters and also three or four months ago by one of our Superiors from America who came here for the Chapter, who had personally known the mother of the Servant of God and a sister.

p. 339

The bearing of the Servant of God was humble not only before personages but also with the Sisters, with whom she was ready to yield in differences of view. Looking at Jesus Christ in the poor, she seemed to wish to make herself small and disappear before them.

I saw that a Sister was so ill as to cause nausea, and the Servant of God rendered her the lowest services. Once, coming from outside and finding her in bed, I made as if to kiss her feet, but she refused and began a talk on humility, protesting that she was nothing and did not wish to be anything.

§ 536
Fame of humility.

Many Priests were surprised to see that the Servant of God went to the Secretariat to give them the first greeting. Of her great humility I heard speak in a special way a Priest of Borgo San Donnino.

Of Mgr. Gaetano Pomarici I heard say: «If the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne has developed rapidly, we Priests can well say that it is due to the great humility of the Foundress». And from many other persons, by word of mouth and in writing, I heard the humility of our Mother Foundress extolled. Among these I recall a Senator, a Prefect, a Bailiff.

Not only on my own part can I affirm that the Servant of God persevered in the exercise of the Theological and Cardinal virtues, of our Vows, and of humility, on which I have deposed, never having perceived in her any stain of fault or of any imperfection, but I can also say in all conscience that from year to year I saw her always progress in the love of God, in detachment from creatures, and in the other virtues enumerated above.

§ 537
She exercised the virtues without exaggeration but in an uncommon way.

Ad 28: The Servant of God exercised all the virtues enumerated above as if they were innate in her, and therefore in the most natural and unaffected way: she exercised them in the highest degree and therefore without hesitation I can say that she exercised them to a heroic degree.

Ad 29: In none of the virtues enumerated above did the Servant of God ever exceed. According to our short views it might seem to us that she exceeded in the virtue of penance and mortification, but it is clear that to her love for this virtue the Lord's aids responded, so that she not only did not become unfit for the office of Mother General, but not even less useful.

p. 340

§ 538
Spirit of prophecy.

Ad 30: I spoke one day to the Servant of God about my brother, who had lost his little children and was desolate, also because he had no hope of being able to have others, owing to his wife's infirmity. The Servant of God assured me that he would have other children, and that the first would be a boy. And so it happened. I shall even say that the little boy they then had is truly a child of blessing, because he succeeds in everything.

Both in the foundations of houses and in the success or not of some Novice, or in the illnesses of some Sister, she showed herself endowed with the spirit of prophecy. If we were alarmed by the difficulties that arose in the foundations, she reassured us with these words: «I guarantee you that this one will succeed».

Sometimes there were splendid offers for foundations of new houses. Her Councillors were for accepting, but she said: «It cannot succeed, it would not succeed; the glory of God is not in it»; and therefore she did not accept. Sometimes I was present at these talks.

§ 539
The book «Labors and Consolations of a Soul».

Ad 32, Proc. fol. 1836v.: Many years ago I read a book entitled «Labors and Consolations of a Soul», which I believe was written by the Servant of God. Once I asked her whether she was the author; she neither denied nor affirmed. By higher ecclesiastical order it was afterward withdrawn from circulation, but I do not know why. I did not even manage to read it all. Of that book there was also a compendium. I found it most beautiful; for my part I saw in it nothing but beautiful things. Besides very many letters of the Servant of God I have also read many elevations of hers on loose sheets, for she, even when occupied in temporal affairs, sometimes interrupted herself to write some thought of elevation to God on any paper, perhaps on the back of a note of accounts or of a letter. I infer from this that she was interrupted, because in the notes of accounts I saw that sometimes the sum was not completed.

At other times in the letters she began with elevations to God, in which one saw that she lingered very willingly, and then confessed she was obliged to interrupt them to deal with the affairs of the house.

I remember in particular one addressed to Sr. Anna Vincenza or Francesca.

I know several prayers of the Servant of God, even printed ones, such as that to the Most Holy Trinity, that to the Eternal Father in the manner of a little chaplet, and yet another to the Eternal Father; I have read others in her manuscripts, but unpublished.

§ 540
No undue cult.

Ad 36: I am not aware of acts of undue cult paid to the Servant of God after her death, such as hanging ex-votos or exposing relics. However, she has had and has much veneration from people of the common folk and of every other social class. The poor, who continued to come to our door for alms, asked for some little keepsake of our Mother, objects that had belonged to the Servant of God, such as a piece of sleeve or other scrap of cloth, which certainly could not serve for use; and these relics were asked for not only by the poor but also by rich persons. I can say that so did all my acquaintances and my pupils, who, not being able to have a piece of an object of the Servant of God, were content with something that had touched something that had belonged to her.

Many sick people in our hospitals, in our boarding schools, commended themselves to the Servant of God, following the knowledge of her virtue given them by our Sisters or by the presidents and administrators of the works to which these are attached. For these presidents, etc., having known the Servant of God, in general never tired of extolling her virtues. This admiration and veneration of which I have spoken, I can say with certainty, never had anything artificial about it, but was always spontaneous and sincere.

Among the personages from whom I heard the Servant of God spoken of with veneration, besides the Cardinal of Belmonte, I heard her spoken of also by four other Cardinals, whom I could not well say now which; and they invited us to follow her holy footsteps.

§ 541
Fame of holiness.

Ad 38: I heard Cardinal Verga many times, speaking of the Servant of God, call her your holy Mother General; Cardinal Pende, Mgr. Chappon, Bishop of Nice, Abbot Fante (I think of Nice), Canon Tosti of Foligno and others, I heard them speak of the Servant of God, during her life, as of a saint. I also heard people of the common folk speak of the Servant of God as of a Saint. When she went on visitation to Palermo, I know they wanted to kiss even her feet. Several chaplains of our Houses, such as those of Borgo San Donnino and of Caltanissetta, said: «Your Mother is certainly a Saint, because when she has made a visit to your houses one sees the traces of it». What happened at Palermo, of wanting to kiss her feet, happened also in Calabria and in other houses of Sicily, as I heard from Sr. A. Melenzia, Superior, I do not know well whether of Cotrone, of Taranto or of Cosenza, and from Mother Bertuzzi.

p. 342

The esteem and veneration for the Servant of God after her death has not only been preserved but has also grown, because one sees that she is not invoked in vain. Many take an interest in the Process, ask whether it has begun, at what point it is, whether we are doing anything; others rejoice that it has already begun, such as the Countess Di Nunzio Maria dei Malatesta. So also many Bishops wish to be kept informed of the work of the Processes; among others the Bishop of Borgo San Donnino, who died recently, Bishop Paolo Tei, also deceased, Mgr. Iorio, formerly Archbishop of Taranto. It can be said that every Superior speaks of her own Bishop as of a person who takes an interest in the Process.

Throughout the Institute, both during her life and after her death, even among the Sisters who never knew her, the esteem and veneration that has always been held for the Servant of God is as for a Saint, and, to say the expression I heard, worthy of a niche (that is, of an altar); and this esteem, both in the Institute and outside, had its basis and origin in the knowledge of the virtues of the Servant of God; knowledge obtained directly, or by means of her works, or from those persons who were fully close to her. And I believe that this esteem is truly just and due.

WITNESS XVI
Very Rev. Mgr. PIETRO TOSTI

Scope in the process: From Sess. 216th of 5 June 1916 (fol. 1852) to Sess. 218th of 7 June 1916 (fol. 1872v.).

Name, surname, date and place of birth: Pietro Tosti, born on 28 April 1859 at Cancellara, near Foligno.

State and profession: Honorary Canon and Chancellor of the Curia of Foligno.

Quality of the witness: Eyewitness.

Age of the witness when he came to know the Servant of God: 36 years.

Age of the Servant of God when the witness came to know her: 64 years.

Age of the witness at the time of the deposition: 57 years.

p. 343

Length of acquaintance and its motivation: The witness came to know the Servant of God in the last five years of her life (1895-1900), having been asked by her to take an interest in the House that the Daughters of St. Anne had at Foligno.

Observations on the witness, on the scope and on the content of the deposition: Given the kind of acquaintance he had, the witness presents the Servant of God to us in the office of Superior General, always watchful over the progress and running of the various houses: through the account of the history of the house at Foligno, he brings to light her dedication and her ponderate way of acting. In answering on the individual virtues and the fame of holiness, the witness shows himself in possession of very interesting proofs.

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 1855v., testis respondit:

§ 542
General particulars of the witness.

My name is Pietro Tosti, of the late Mattia and Cecilia Nardi. I was born at Cancellara, near Foligno, on 28 April 1859. At nine years of age I was placed in the Seminary by my parents, and I was ordained Priest on 19 May 1883. I taught elementary school in the Seminary, I was first Mansionary and then effective Canon, and, having tendered my resignation of the Canonry, I was named Honorary Canon. As soon as I had celebrated my first Mass I was named Vice-Chancellor, and after 14 years Chancellor of the Curia of Foligno. I was named Honorary Secret Chaplain of His Holiness Pope Pius the Tenth, then confirmed by the present Pontiff Benedict XV.

§ 543
Scope of acquaintance.

Ad 7: I came to know the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno personally five years before she died, Mgr. Faloci, Vicar General of the Diocese, having assigned me from then on as Ordinary Confessor of her small Community; and I was much in correspondence with her, by letter too, to improve the situation of her house in Foligno, which was not known and was neglected by the citizens.

Of the Servant of God there spoke to me the late engineer Giovanni Bertuzzi, the Marchioness Costanza Bernabò, likewise deceased, who had a real cult for her, Mrs. Anna Maria Bartolomei Castori, living, and Mrs. Countess, I think, Vittoria Orfini, deceased.

Ad 8: Already before knowing the Servant of God personally, I had known the spirit of holiness in her daughters who were at Foligno, and I told myself that so much spirit and so much heroism could not be in those Sisters if the Foundress were not a Saint; and when I had known her personally, she confirmed me in that esteem, which I have always kept joined to devotion; therefore in my prayers I commend myself very often to her. I should rejoice much if she were raised to the honor of the Altars, and in the hope that this may happen, I have already planned to put her image in my Shrine of St. Mary of the Weeping.

§ 544
Faithful to the duty of visiting the communities.

Ad 23: I know that the Servant of God observed the obligation of visiting her houses with great diligence, and that, when she was prevented by illness, she was afflicted, and the illness must have been very grave for her to abstain. So I learned from the Sisters themselves, and I could not determine the names; from them I also learned that she was not easy in the admission of postulants, that she studied them to see whether they were truly conformed to the spirit she desired, after already having received them on the information she had had from Parish Priests and Bishops, for whom she had a profound reverence and wanted her Sisters to have it, joined to blind obedience.

I remember that she wanted me to inform the Bishop of everything and to seek his opinion about the House of Foligno. I remember that she never failed at Christmas to pay her respects to the Bishop by letter, and wanted her Sisters to do the same.

§ 545
Prudence in the choice of superiors.

She had no scruple about changing personnel in the various houses when she judged it opportune. I remember that in the last year, and precisely in February of the year 1900, when I came to her in Rome to speak to her about her house at Foligno, and told her that one of the things that had made some impression about her Institute was the frequent change of personnel, she, pointing me to a drawer of her little table, said to me: «You are right, but this drawer is witness that I try to make the changes with good reason. If you knew how many anonymous letters, how many criticisms this drawer contains! Criticisms from respectable personages and even from Bishops...! I too must obey the Bishops, I too must take account of so many circumstances! Ah, if you saw this drawer, which I may call the drawer of my sorrows, you would not wonder at the changes! I do not complain, however, because if I am to go to Paradise, I must earn it, and besides the work of God is perfected in contradictions».

The Superiors she chose for the houses, first of all she wanted them to be very attached to the rule. Naturally, in the beginning, she did not have enough Sisters who had this chief quality and that of good administrators who knew how to keep the books of administration well; and then the less cultured and less intelligent she sent to the smaller houses. I never heard from anyone that the least reproach was made to her in the choice of Sisters for the various offices.

§ 546
She cared for the health of the sisters.

I myself verified how much care and how much promptness she had for the health of her Sisters. As soon as she came to know that any of those at Foligno was not feeling well, by letter or telegram she called her to Rome, having her accompanied too, if the poor state of health required it. And here in Rome then she provided according to the cases, regardless of expense. I remember having heard her say once to the Superior of Foligno, to whom she was speaking of the care of a Sister: «If you have not the means, I shall see to it».

Now I shall tell the history of the house of Foligno, in which the figure of the Servant of God is reflected.

This is one of the first houses of the Institute, and the Servant of God came here for the first time to found the house, when she was not yet dressed as a Religious. The occasion of her coming to Foligno was having been invited by the Princess of Piombino to open a small house with a nursery school at Uppello, barely two or three miles from Foligno. The Princess offered her a most modest house, so that they might help the Parish Priest in the catechetical instruction of the children. She promised much, but obtained very little. I do not know whether other reasons were added to this one. The Servant of God found herself obliged, after a very short time, to leave Uppello; and then she settled at Foligno, buying a most modest house from the two Grampini Sisters, with whom she made a life annuity agreement, that is, they ceded their house to her, and she bound herself to maintain them. At Foligno they were little welcomed at first, through the work of Freemasonry, and the people were made to believe that these Sisters were a kind of spies of the Jesuits, and that they were sent under the pretext of charity to discover the affairs of families.

They had come around 1870.

In this first house of Foligno the following event occurred.

§ 547
Conversion of a sick man and vengeance against the Servant of God.

In those first days, when the Servant of God, the house having been opened, was staying in Foligno, she was invited to assist a dying young man, a victim of his vices and so hostile to religion that he had himself guarded by two friends, lest the Priest should come in to him. The first nights the Servant of God confined herself to the bodily care of the sick man, to win his soul. And she succeeded so well in her aim that he proposed to confess, and before that he wanted at every moment to kiss the Crucifix. But how could a Priest enter? The Servant of God asked him when those guards would leave him, even for a little while; and he answered that not before one or two after midnight. And she, having made the opportune arrangements with the Parish Priest of the Cathedral, had him pass by the sick man in those free hours, and the patient confessed with such jubilation of heart that he could scarcely contain himself and, full of contentment, exclaimed: «Now I am happy»; and he always wanted to kiss the Crucifix that the Servant of God held.

After this event the sick man felt a kind of aversion to his two guards, and could no longer bear them near him, and he gave the Servant of God to understand it, and she gave him courage to send them away. And he made known to them that he now had that Lady, who assisted him well, and that there was no more need of their services. And so he dismissed them.

They understood that some change in a religious sense had taken place. They wished to take vengeance on the Servant of God. They therefore waited for her one morning at about five, when she was coming out of the sick man's house to go and hear Mass in the Cathedral, and one of them rushed at her with a dagger. The Servant of God fled crying out, and that scoundrel did not have the courage to finish her. A few days later the Servant of God was summoned by the Vice-Prefect, or I do not know what other Magistrate, who urged her to leave Foligno, since her work was so disliked by the population. But she answered: «I should understand your invitation if I did evil; and if I do good, it is quite natural that I should suffer something!». The police did not move, and everything returned to silence, until some time later, when another event occurred, of which I shall speak in the next session.

Proc. fol. 1866: Shortly after the event of the attempt with the dagger on the Servant of God, which I narrated in the preceding session, another occurred.

§ 548
Another case of persecution: fortitude of the Servant of God.

One night, shortly after midnight, fire was set to the door of the Sisters' house. They heard noise, looked out of the window, and seeing the flames at the door of the house, began to cry out, but no one was passing at that moment, and no one came. The Servant of God then went down with her Sisters and with them set about putting out the fire. Three or four times there passed before the door, while they toiled to put it out, an evil-looking fellow, who looked on but did not help. I would almost say he took pleasure in the embarrassment in which he saw those Sisters. The Sisters succeeded in putting out the fire, and found near the door a placard on which was written: «We do not want these prostitutes in Foligno, kept by the Duke of Sora and by Count Morotti» (who was a well-known staunch Catholic). The next morning the Servant of God reported the matter to the police station, the Magistrate then summoned her to examine her, but nothing came of it. The Servant of God left deeply impressed, and did not want to return any more. I then induced her to promise me to return to Foligno, where she would have found festive welcomes, but shortly afterward death came upon her, and so she never came again. She had remained so impressed, she told me, that when she wanted to correct some Religious she threatened to transfer her to Foligno; and she was about to withdraw her Sisters when I took the matter in hand and succeeded in making the work prosper.

The two events that I have narrated, the last of the preceding session and that of this session, I learned from various persons of Foligno, from the Sisters of the House and from the Servant of God herself. Of this last I also read the report that was made by the Magistrate of the King's Prosecutor's Office. And of this report there must be a copy at this Generalate House; and I succeeded in obtaining it for her after three years of insistent requests.

Of the two events referred to above Professor Carlo Botti made an oil painting. This Professor was enthusiastic about the Servant of God, and spoke of her with profound admiration and veneration, as of a saint of the Altar, as I myself heard, and he added further: «That is a woman who in time will go to the Altars».

For the development of the work the Servant of God had to leave the House of Signora Grampini and transferred, after ten or fifteen years, her Community to the Barbetti House, where she paid as rent one lira a day, and there she remained until 1898. When in 1895 I was named Confessor of that small Community, I became gradually persuaded that it was a work worthy of greater development. I came to know the spirit of those Sisters, which left me full of admiration.

Their first Superior had died in the reputation of a saint, and her body remained exposed for two days, the people flocking to pray. Some Sisters had left their lives there amid extraordinary sacrifices, and the people declared them victims of charity.

§ 549
God's protection over the work of the Servant of God.

And now I shall tell of the purchase of the house in which the Sisters still are, because there are circumstances that reveal how Providence watched over the works of Gattorno.

For the further development of the work of Gattorno in Foligno I had planned, and persuaded the Servant of God to buy, a more suitable house.

A house having come up for public auction which seemed to me most suitable for the purpose, and having obtained the necessary faculties from the Servant of God, I had the bidding take place in Perugia. Of this auction a man of Foligno who was in love with that house had not become aware, and he would not have let it escape him even for twenty thousand lire, a sum which he offered after the definitive award. And that although he was employed in the tax office, and right in his own office the notice of the said auction had been posted. It was awarded to the Servant of God for six thousand five hundred lire. But after the definitive award various offers were made to me and to the Servant of God that it should be ceded to them, and these offers ranged from twelve to sixteen and to twenty thousand lire. I must note that the Sisters had received from Marquis Ugolino Barnabò five thousand lire in gratitude for assistance given him during about two months of grave illness; and I, when I proposed to the Servant of God the purchase of a house, allowed myself to remind her that the people of Foligno had also given something to her Sisters. The Servant of God answered me: «Yes, it is true, and those five thousand lire I keep always intact, awaiting an occasion to pour them out for the benefit of Foligno». And although she could have told me so, she did not add that the house of Foligno was almost entirely at the charge of the Generalate House.

§ 550
Apostolic Visitation under accusation of bad administration.

Ad 25: Of the Apostolic Visitation, with which Mgr. Serafini, now Cardinal, was charged, I can say that I learned from various Sisters that it was originated by the many, many petitions of ecclesiastical and lay personages, and also of Sisters, against the Servant of God, accusing her of not keeping the administration of the Institute well, of squandering, of keeping up a certain display while she let the Sisters lack even the necessary; accusations that the Apostolic Visitation afterward showed to be unfounded. I saw and spoke with the Visitor when, already Archbishop of Spoleto, he came to visit, as the last, the house of Foligno; with that visit, as he expressed himself to me, he remained fully satisfied, and gave me the most flattering praises of the whole Community. Here I can add that similar praises of the Community I heard from the Visitor of the Diocese, Mgr. Giovanni Maria Santarelli, Archbishop of Urbino. Who in particular said to me: «This is one of the few Religious houses where I found all hearts in unison».

Ad 26: My conviction, formed from what I saw and heard said, is that Gattorno scrupulously observed always, throughout her life, the commandments of God and of the Church and the obligations of her various states.

Ad 27: I can say also with the same conviction that the Servant of God possessed and exercised the Theological and Cardinal virtues and their related ones.

§ 551
Faith and union with God.

The spirit that the Servant of God instilled in her Sisters for saving souls has something extraordinary, not only for the prayers they said, but also for the sacrifices to which they aspired for the salvation of souls. From her speaking I saw her always, I would say, eager to do great good. She prayed much, and from her Sisters I learned that when they went to bed in the evening, she on the contrary often went to the Church in secret, where sometimes she stayed the whole night.

I have it well in mind: when she conversed with me, I saw in it her union with God, even when it was a matter of business, so that she inspired devotion in me.

Of her particular devotions I can say that she had very great devotion to the Most Holy Trinity, to St. Anne and to St. Francis of Assisi. Of this last devotion I heard speak from the late Mother Carrega, who told me that the Servant of God, from the foundation, had placed the Institute under the protection of this Saint, because she desired it rich in poverty, and that her ardent desire in life had always been to be able to open a house near the tomb of St. Francis. (A desire that she could not see fulfilled, and in her homage Mother Carrega herself fulfilled it).

In speaking she was seen to be very zealous for the decorum of the House of God, and willingly entered into conversation with me on what she had done for her Church, and expressed to me the desire that I should celebrate at the Altar of St. Anne.

§ 552
Hope and trust in the Lord.

Proc. fol. 1875: I cannot say much of her Hope, except that when I heard her speak of her Institute she said: «The difficulties are many, but God will certainly not abandon me and my Daughters». She exhorted me to continue working, assuring me of the reward from the Lord. I now recall that, having been attacked because I was concerned with her Sisters at Foligno, the Servant of God, learning of it, wrote to me, and I remember well these words, which made much impression on me: «Be most tranquil, because against St. Anne no one can prevail».

In difficulties I always found her very calm; she discussed them, yes, but went forward with an admirable assurance.

As to detachment from temporal goods, she was completely detached. So her conversation and the virtues of her Sisters made me believe.

Of her charity toward God I have already said what I knew, speaking of the virtue of faith.

I have said much also of her charity toward her neighbor, and I can add that I heard her recommend to her Sisters to help the Parish Priests in catechetical instruction for first Communions, and not to do it for any compensation.

She did not want to return to Foligno, not out of resentment against that City, but only for the impression suffered in the events recalled above, and when I proposed to her my plans for enlarging her work in that City, she answered me: «Do and say as you wish; I am in your hands».

She was moreover most grateful for my devoting myself to the benefit of her Sisters at Foligno.

§ 553
Prudence, temperance, penance.

I noted her Prudence, because before entrusting herself to me she wished to know me well, and at the beginning of our relations I saw her very reserved and cautious, until she had come to know well that I was wholly for her Religious.

When I asked for the change of some Superior, because she was not suitable for our City, she asked me for time to reflect and pray.

p. 351

I know that she ate very little and very ordinary foods. I heard from her Sisters that she spent the greater part of the night in prayer.

Her Sisters further spoke to me of many instruments of penance of hers at Piacenza, and that there, for a bed, a very modest pallet and a wooden cross were found.

I no longer know which Sister told me that the Servant of God in her last illness, after repeated insistence from the doctor who wanted to examine her properly, and she refused, finally asked for time to consult first the Confessor; from whom having received obedience, she resigned herself, and the doctor discovered that she wore a chain about her hips, which had sunk into the flesh.

When she had taken a resolution, and believed it for the good of the Institute, there were no recommendations or influences that could avail to turn her aside, using however every regard and courtesy.

§ 554
Poor, humble, obedient.

The poverty of the Servant of God, as I heard from her Sisters, besides from her love of St. Francis of Assisi, was noticeable even in the crockery she used for herself at table: for a glass she had a bowl of the commonest earthenware.

I noticed that, while for herself she wanted no regard, no compliment, no courtesy, she desired however that her Assistants and the Secretary be treated with regard, and was pleased when she saw them so treated.

Toward Ecclesiastical Authority I noticed in her an obedience and reverence, I would almost say exaggerated.

In her bearing she was most modest though always dignified.

In all the virtues enumerated above, whether Theological, Cardinal or related, I have absolute conviction that the Servant of God not only persevered to the end but indeed went on always growing in them.

Ad 28: I believe her a Saint of the Altar, and although I do not know all the particulars of her virtues, I consequently have the conviction that she had them to a heroic degree, a conviction born in me first because I have known some of her Sisters who were truly heroines.

§ 555
She never exceeded in the exercise of the virtues.

Ad 29: I do not believe that the Servant of God ever exceeded in the exercise of the virtues so as to render herself unfit for her office. She worked always to the end, and worked even too much, and it is the common persuasion that she shortened her life through excessive work.

Ad 34: I attended the funeral of the Servant of God, which was splendid and moving, through the weeping and desolation of the Sisters. The crowd was so great that the Church was not enough to contain it, and it was a crowd of every class.

Ad 38: At Foligno the Servant of God is known more through her work than for herself, having remained there very little. The work has been universally extolled. Of the Servant of God, all the persons who knew her, or whom I asked, painted her to me as a Saint, but I do not know whether they meant a Saint of the Altar; and to some of them, to whom I said that I would come to Rome for the Process of the Servant of God: «Ah, yes, — they told me —, she was a Saint».

WITNESS XVII (II ex officio)

Most Excellent and Most Reverend PIETRO ALFONSO IORIO

Scope in the process: Sess. 221st of 14 June 1916 (fol. 1892v.).

State and profession: Titular Archbishop of Nicomedia, consultor of the Congregations of the Consistory, of the Council, of the Sacraments, of Regulars and of Rites.

Quality of the witness: Eyewitness.

Age of the Servant of God when the witness came to know her: 58 years.

Length of acquaintance and its motivation: The witness came to know the Servant of God when she, in 1889, arrived at Taranto to open a house of the Institute.

Observations on the witness, on the scope and on the content of the deposition: On the basis of the relations he had with the Sisters and of what he directly knows through the meetings he had, the witness is convinced that the Servant of God carried out very profitably her office of Superior General; indeed, giving a judgment on the virtues, he declares he never found any defect in her.

§ 556
General particulars of the witness and scope of acquaintance.

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 1896, testis respondit:

My name is Pietro Alfonso Iorio, of the late Donato and Maria Trocchia. I was born at Sant'Angelo in Cancelli, Diocese of Benevento. I was ordained Priest in 1865 and consecrated Bishop of Lacedonia on 7 March 1880; then promoted to the Archbishopric of Taranto

p. 353

in the Consistory of 27 March 1885; transferred to the titular Archiepiscopal See of Nicomedia in November 1908. I was named Vicar of the Vatican Basilica and then of the Lateran one, and Consultor of the Congregations of the Consistory, of the Council, of the Sacraments, of Regulars and of Rites.

Ad 7: In 1889 a house of the Daughters of St. Anne was opened at Taranto; for this reason I came to know and had relations with the Servant of God, Rosa Gattorno. I also heard of her from her Sisters at Taranto, such as for example: Sr. A. Ermelinda Bianchi, now Provincial, Sr. A. Cunegonda Pacini, then Superior of that house at Taranto, still living, and others. I also heard of her from the Sisters of the Generalate House, such as Sr. A. Carrega, Sr. A. Celsa Speranza, Sr. A. Camilla Valentini, Sr. A. Santina Solenghi. I do not remember what other persons spoke to me of her.

After the death of the Servant of God I read some funeral oration, but in my deposition I shall keep only to what I saw or heard.

§ 557
Esteem of the Servant of God for her prudence.

Ad 8: From the first moment I knew her I conceived great esteem for the Servant of God, because I at once noticed the wisdom and prudence with which she was endowed, and that she was not an ordinary woman.

Afterward, having had occasion to deal with her, my esteem for her grew much and widened until it almost became admiration. I should therefore rejoice if she were raised to the honor of the Altars.

I must also say that I did not know her intimately.

§ 558
Enthusiasm of the sisters for the virtue of the Servant of God.

Ad 22: I have always heard it said that Mother Gattorno was always Superior General of her Institute. From her Sisters, none excepted, I always heard her spoken of very well; therefore I formed the conviction that she carried out her office very well.

I know that she visited her houses. I am not sure, but I think I saw her four or five times at Taranto.

I heard her Sisters praise her much for her great charity toward the sick Sisters, for the affectionate way in which she received them, and the like. I never heard that any complained that the Servant of God made them lack the necessary.

Ad 26: Of the virtues of the Servant of God I know no particular. I can say that I never saw in her any defect, for the little I dealt with her; I never had cause to complain of her and she was always very deferential toward me. And when, therefore, after her death, I heard the many praises that were said of her, and then afterward read the Articles of the Postulator of the Cause, I was not at all surprised, and indeed I had every reason to believe what I was told and read. Many facts may still have been reported to me by her Sisters, but I do not now recall them.

All the sisters with whom I spoke, and of whom I spoke above, hold her a saint who perhaps might even be canonized. From authoritative persons I never heard the Servant of God spoken ill of.

WITNESS XVIII
Rev. Fr. VINCENZO DA ALATRI

Scope in the process: From Sess. 222nd of 17 June 1916 (fol. 1901) to Sess. 226th of 4 July 1916 (fol. 1932).

Name, surname, date and place of birth: Sisto (surname illegible to me), born at Alatri on 3 September 1850.

State and profession: Capuchin Religious, chaplain in the convent of the Conception in Rome.

Quality of the witness: Eyewitness.

Age of the witness when he came to know the Servant of God: 47 years.

Age of the Servant of God when the witness came to know her: 66 years.

Age of the witness at the time of the deposition: 66 years.

Length of acquaintance and its motivation: The witness came to know Gattorno in 1897, having been named confessor of the Community of the Generalate House; from then on he was spiritually close to her, assisting her always until the evening before her death, that is, until the evening of 5 May 1900.

Observations on the witness, on the scope and on the content of the deposition: To the three years of acquaintance with the Servant of God the witness joins a frequency of contacts that is reflected in a deposition which brings to light the principal questions of her life and her spirituality. He emphasizes the peculiar gifts of an enlightened guide of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne and examines some thorny questions that caused the intervention of the Apostolic Visitor. The verification of the practice of the virtues enables the witness to justify his judgment on heroicity. The events relating to the death are well illustrated, since the witness himself administered Extreme Unction to Mother Rosa. Lastly, the witness does not fail to let us know his own thought on the fame of holiness. What the witness affirms of a positive kind he verified personally or learned from persons worthy of faith: the negative statements arise from personal resentments (cf. foll. 1935-1936). Consequently everything that does not touch his hypersensitive susceptibility is to be held as true: when he is personally involved, he is not reliable.

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 1904v., testis respondit:

§ 559
General particulars of the witness and scope of acquaintance. Prudent in the fulfilment of her duty as superior.

In the world I was called Sisto Macciveca, of the late Giovanni Battista and Santa Ciangola. In Religion my name is Vincenzo da Alatri.

I was born at Alatri on 3 September 1850. I entered the Religious Order of the Capuchin Fathers at 18 years, and professed solemnly 4 years later. I was ordained Priest in 1874. I have been Preceptor of our Novices, Vicar and Chaplain of our infirmary in Rome at the Convent of the Conception, where I have been for 40 years.

Ad 7: I first knew the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno in June 1897, having been named Confessor of the Community of this Generalate House. After a six-year term, I remained here always as Chaplain.

Ad 22: I have heard it said that the Servant of God was always Mother General of her Institute until death, which office she always held with much diligence and prudence. I never heard it said that she was lax in a bad sense in the acceptance of Postulants. I was able to see myself, however, that when the Postulants did not have the required qualities and aptitudes, she sent them away.

Also in my time, although in poor health, she went to visit the houses and was absent from the generalate house for two or three months.

I heard from some Sisters, whom I do not even know and who came to this house in passing, partialities attributed to the Servant of God in her government. But I never heard anything similar from the Sisters Carrega, Speranza, etc., named above.

I heard it said that the surpluses of the other houses came to this generalate house, while on the other hand they were helped, in case of need, by this generalate house, and I saw many times the sacristy being emptied to help the poor houses. Someone, but I do not know who she was, unburdened herself to me saying that in her house the food was too measured because the Superior wanted to look good before the Mother General; but I believe they tried not to let the Mother General know.

§ 561
Complaints about the relations of the Servant of God with her relatives.

Ad 24: Sr. A. Santina Solenghi or Sr. A. Michelina Negri (certainly no other), outside the Confessional, sometimes complained to me that many things passed to the relatives, who were in the adjoining dwelling. «Parcels come, they told me, and the best things pass to them». They told me further that the Servant of God many times knew nothing of it.

I heard many complaints from the Sisters, almost all of this Generalate house, about the too great coming and going of the relatives, and the older little niece went about the whole house. I know that the Servant of God sometimes made some reproof to the little niece because she wandered about the house. But I never knew that the relatives, little nephews, made noise in the corridors.

I heard it said that certain Superiors, when they sent parcels of foodstuffs to the Mother General, wrote not only to her but also to the daughter, warning her that they had sent such a parcel to the Servant of God, and that naturally there was a share for them too. So the relatives, when the parcels arrived, were already warned, and knew what they contained, and carried them off, saying that they already knew what they contained and that they had already arranged with the Servant of God. So at least sometimes, as I learned from Sr. A. Santina Solenghi and from Sr. A. Serafina Foglia.

I also heard complaint that the Servant of God paid the boarding fee for her little niece at the Child Jesus, and they asked each other: «Where did this money come from?».

I heard from almost all the Sisters of this house that the construction of this house and of the adjoining Church was entrusted by the Servant of God to her Brother Federico, who, they said, must have profited also for himself. And this I also heard from Sr. A. Serafina Foglia.

§ 562
Reason for and course of the Apostolic Visitation.

Ad 25, Proc. fol. 1911v.: Of the Apostolic Visitation I know that it was made by Abbot Serafini, now Cardinal. The reason was the petitions made to the Holy See because, according to what I heard, in the houses of this Institute a bit of gossip reigned.

Fr. Luigi da Sezze, my Confrere and predecessor in the office of Confessor in this Community, told me that he had worked hard that an Apostolic Visitor should be sent to this Institute, but he too told me that they were not grave matters, but gossip.

I must add that Fr. Luigi da Sezze seemed to me hand in glove with Count Barbiellini, son-in-law of Mother Gattorno. Some times I saw that Barbiellini came to the Convent to speak with Fr. Luigi, and Barbiellini himself, after the death of Mother Gattorno, or when about to die, told me that Fr. Luigi had favored him in many things in his relations with Mother Gattorno, in interests and also to obtain board.

Sr. A. Serafina Foglia told me that the Apostolic Visitor at Piacenza had a door of communication closed with the adjoining house of the Barbiellini, through which he passed with his family to enter the Monastery, as also at the time of the Apostolic Visitation a similar communication was closed between this Generalate house and the adjoining one of the relatives of Mother Gattorno.

Mgr. Felice Sarra, who sometimes accompanied Mgr. Serafini to this house as a friend, and therefore without taking part in any way in the Visitation itself, told me that the Apostolic Visitor had remedied many inconveniences. I would not know what value to give to these words, because he never told me he had learned it from the Visitor.

I know from Sr. A. Serafina Foglia that the Apostolic Visitation at first was a sorrow for Mother Gattorno, and I know no more.

Ad 26: It is not even worth speaking of the observance of the Commandments of God, of the Church and of the obligations of her state, so persuaded am I of it.

Ad 27: I believe that the Servant of God possessed and exercised not only the theological virtues but also the Cardinal ones, and the others, such as Poverty, Chastity, obedience and humility.

§ 563
Living faith.

From the fact of her great penance, of which I shall speak later, and from other virtues, it can be gathered that the faith of the Servant of God was living. She inculcated in her Sisters not only to instruct themselves in Christian doctrine but also to teach it to others.

In the little chaplet to the Eternal Father composed by Mother Gattorno one sees how she prayed and wanted her daughters to pray for sinners and for the Holy Church.

She was assiduous in prayer, and it may be said that she was always in the Chapel: I saw her many times, and always noticed her absorbed in God.

§ 564
Practice of confession, prayer and devotions.

She ordinarily confessed every week, and when occasion arose, on the occasion of wishing to be reconciled. She was very brief in her confession, and outside the Confessional it was very rare for me to meet and speak with the Servant of God, except on some occasion, I would say official, such as Christmas, Easter, St. Anne, etc.

In the Chapel I always saw her kneeling on the prie-dieu and never seated, and she always kept her hands joined. If the Servant of God ever missed Mass through illness, otherwise she never missed it. This I say at least for the time when she was in Rome. Every day the Servant of God received Communion, and it was noticed then that she was as if raised up in God.

She had a special devotion to the Eternal Father, so much so that she prescribed to her Institute the pious practices of a month in his honor. From Sr. A. Serafina I heard that she was very devoted to the Heart of Jesus, to St. Francis of Assisi, to St. Francis of Paola, to St. Michael the Archangel, to Our Lady of Lourdes and to Mary Mater Gratiae, and to St. Anne. In honor of these she wanted an altar erected in the Church of this House.

As to devotion to the Child Jesus, she had it great, for I saw that she had the crib made in the room of the Congregation of the Daughters of Mary. On Christmas night I know that Fr. Agostino Donadio celebrated in this house.

In Holy Week she saw to it that the Holy Sepulchre was made in the Church with much decorum. In the Chapel adjoining this room a Crucifix is exhibited which, Mother Carrega told me, had spoken to the Servant of God.

In this Church of the Generalate House the Servant of God wanted the months of January for the Eternal Father, of March for St. Joseph, of May for Our Lady, June for the Sacred Heart of Jesus, July for St. Anne, October for Our Lady of the Rosary, November for the Dead and December for the Holy Child to be kept, and moreover she wanted Novenas for Holy Christmas, for the Immaculate Conception, for Pentecost, for Sts. Peter and Paul, for St. Anne; and Triduums for St. Michael, for St. Francis of Assisi, for St. Francis of Paola and for the Stigmata of St. Francis. She also wanted the Procession for Corpus Christi, and the Sisters, for this devotion of hers, made her a gift of a truly marvelous canopy.

The Church of this Generalate House she wanted dedicated to Mary Mater Gratiae, Mater Misericordiae.

She wanted the whole Institute to fast on the vigil of St. Anne. For her devotion to the Holy Child she provided herself with the faculty of having Masses celebrated on Christmas night throughout the Institute. She also obtained the privilege of the Portiuncula of 2 August for all the houses.

§ 565
Deferential toward authorities.

Proc. fol. 1918v.: The Servant of God was deferential to Authority, and Pius IX honored her with a certain familiarity, as I heard from Fr. Agostino Donadio and from the Sisters.

With the Bishop of Piacenza, Mgr. Scalabrini, there was at first some divergence, as I heard from Sr. A. Serafina Foglia, but then everything was smoothed over, and Mgr. Scalabrini was afterward a benefactor of the Institute, and when he came to Rome, in the last years of Mother Gattorno, he was a guest of this Generalate House. To the Bishops she was always obedient, as I heard from the Sisters. She was respectful and deferential to all Ecclesiastics.

§ 566
Hope and trust in the Lord.

As to Hope, I myself heard the Servant of God, on the occasion of something adverse to the Institute, exclaim: «Fiat voluntas tua». Money she considered only as a means of doing good, and she had, as the Sisters told me, a great deal. Nevertheless in the beginning of the Institute she found herself in some straits, and from the Sisters I heard that unexpectedly sometimes Providence came through her prayers. About herself she thought neither little nor much, and if the Sisters, as I heard from them, had not been around her to make her give up a worn-out habit, it would always have been the same.

Her trust was placed principally in God, yet she did not neglect human aids, as opportunity offered, and so she made use of her brother Federico in various cases.

§ 567
Love of God and of neighbor.

Certainly the Servant of God had much charity toward the Lord. And this she showed in her continual vigilance over herself to avoid offense to God, even the slightest; and in the three years in which I confessed her I was able to verify that God was not only all her hope but also all her love. She could say that God was her pars et reliquia.

When her Sisters came, she said to them: «Daughters, put your trust in God, and do not lose heart, however many contrary events may arise»; and she exhorted them to prayer. And I myself sometimes was present at these exhortations.

When she was in the Chapel, I noticed that her eyes were always fixed on the Tabernacle; and I saw that when she was in the Chapel she always had a flushed face.

Of charity toward neighbor the Servant of God had so much. And this was toward the shamefaced poor, whom she helped with much consideration.

I heard from the Sisters that she helped not only in money but also in food and clothing. At the solemnities of Easter and above all at Christmas she distributed pasta and sausages, besides the customary bread, and I saw it too with my own eyes, and was amazed at the great quantity.

She helped naturally first of all her poorest houses. Her charity toward the sick is already revealed by the founding of her Institute; but moreover she gave every care to her sick daughters and wanted them to be treated very well.

§ 568
Prudent and just in acting.

As to Prudence, I heard from the Sisters that she asked, in important matters, the counsel of her Assistants; and from the Sisters too I heard that others, having great esteem for her, turned to her for counsel. Of me too she asked counsel sometimes, but about small things.

Since Sr. A. Serafina Foglia was and is held to be a simple soul, the Servant of God often questioned her on certain things to hear what came out of that simple mouth. Sometimes she said to her: «But be quiet, you understand nothing»; but meanwhile she ended by following Sr. A. Serafina's opinion, as she herself told me.

As to Justice, the Servant of God not only paid what she owed but was also generous, although she could not bear waste.

p. 361

Both in manner and in substance, she always showed herself grateful for the benefits done to her and to her Institute.

§ 569
Mortified and temperate.

The Servant of God was most temperate in food. She always ate meatless. Sr. A. Borromea, who was her particular cook, tried to prepare for her the best food, and when sometimes she thought she had prepared the best for her, it was precisely then that the Servant of God did not eat of it, thus leaving Sr. A. Borromea and Mother Carrega in desolation.

She did not want luxury foods, and when the two Sisters mentioned prepared some of these, she left them, and I believe she did it by mortification.

She was temperate not only in quality but also in quantity. As to clothes, she was clean, but as I said she loved old things, and her Sisters had to replace them secretly. And many of the remnants of the habits of the Servant of God ended up on Sr. A. Serafina Foglia, who wore them with devotion, altering them a little, which was not difficult for her, since she was very short in stature.

From Sr. A. Serafina I heard that the Servant of God, before I came here, performed most severe penances. When I came, she had already declined much in health. The one who knew everything of her penances was Fr. Bernardino da Porto Gruaro, as I heard from the Sisters, and I believe he had forbidden her to manifest her penances any more to any Confessor, because to me she never said anything in the three years that I confessed her.

§ 570
Chastity and humility.

Proc. fol. 1926v.: As to Chastity, I can say that she was so reserved that, if she had had strict need of some personal service, the only one to whom she allowed it was Sr. A. Serafina Foglia, as I heard from her herself. She was most modest in her eyes, in her bearing, in everything.

I always heard from the Sisters that when something was imposed on her that did not please her, she nevertheless submitted.

The Servant of God was most humble in bearing, in words, from which one understood that they came from a humble heart. Yet she was at the same time so dignified that she inspired awe, even in me. She was slow and grave, and measured in words.

p. 362

In all the virtues enumerated above the Servant of God always remained constant, and certainly never drew back, and in the love of God, which embraces all the virtues, she was ever more inflamed.

Ad 28: As to the degree of the virtues of the Servant of God, I would not know how to pronounce. Certainly she exercised them in an uncommon way, and as if they were connatural to her, and I could say nothing else.

§ 571
Last illness and serene death.

Ad 33: The Servant of God died on 6 May 1900, at nine o'clock in the morning, and I assisted her always until the evening before.

Toward the end of her life she had so many ailments upon her, but what determined her death I could not specify.

On the evening of the fifth, when I entered the room of the Servant of God, where I also found Fr. Agostino Donadio, I saw that she was approaching the end, and since she could no longer speak, we doubted whether she could receive the Viaticum. Sr. A. Camilla Valentini asked her whether she was content to receive it, and having received an affirmative sign, I brought it to her, and she received the sacred host well; then I administered Extreme Unction to her. Fr. Agostino, who in the preceding days had assisted her, left to me the administration of the last Sacraments because he would have been too moved. At the administration of the Sacraments Mr. Federico, brother of the Servant of God, was present, and in the adjoining room was Abbot Serafini, now Cardinal. Sr. A. Amante La Barbera did not leave the bedside of the Servant of God any more, and read to her the prayers of thanksgiving after the Viaticum. Late, having left Fr. Agostino to assist the Servant of God, I withdrew to a room to rest a little, but after barely three quarters of an hour I was called, the end being feared imminent, because blood was coming from her mouth; but it was only that her denture had shifted and the clasps had wounded her palate and gums. Sr. Serafina Foglia, who understood the matter, removed the denture, and all ended there; and so we came to nine o'clock of the sixth.

About half an hour before, I began to read the commendation of the soul, and she placidly expired. Sr. A. Serafina Foglia and Sr. A. Amante La Barbera, as soon as the Servant of God expired, and other Sisters present, then threw themselves upon the Servant of God, as if they wished to hold back her soul, and remained so for some time weeping.

Two or three of the most capable then remained alone to render the last services to the body, and among these I recall Sr. A. Rosella Bolognini, also deceased, and Sr. A. Serafina; and they then laid her out on the very bed on which she had expired.

Present at the death, of the relatives there was only Count Barbiellini; then the others came also. The impression I received of the presence of Count Gaspare was that he was there only to be able to seize some object. The Servant of God, when she died, was very, very swollen, and dead she emitted much drool from her mouth, which they had to wipe every moment. The photograph was taken, which however came out badly.

Ad 34: The Servant of God remained exposed in that room two days, and many people came to see her: however access was left free only to acquaintances, but to the people of the surrounding area, who also asked to enter, it was not permitted.

§ 572
Funeral and burial.

Ad 35: The brother of the Servant of God, Francesco, was charged with the three coffins and with all the rest for the funeral. Carried into the Church, solemn funeral rites were held for her with the attendance of many people, who were present. I think that among those present was also Mgr. Sardi, Archbishop, still living, and also other respectable persons, both Ecclesiastics and lay.

In the afternoon hours the body was transported to the Campo Santo, and many people took part in carriages. Among others Count Barbiellini with his family. At the Campo Santo was also Mr. Federico, brother of the Servant of God. Here she was first laid in the sepulchre of the Institute in the quadriporticus, and some years later she was transported in procession to the new tomb on the Pincetto.

§ 573
Visits to the tomb. Fame of holiness.

Ad 37: I went many times to the Tomb of the Servant of God out of devotion of her Sisters, who go there often. Those who leave for distant places, as for America, first go to the tomb of their Mother to pray that she may assist them.

Ad 38: I know that the Servant of God, during her life, was esteemed as a holy Religious, but I do not know that she was held as a Saint of the Altar; and this same I say of after her death. But among her Sisters whom I have known they esteem her as a Saint of the Altar, and among her most intimate ones, such as Sr. A. Serafina, Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega, etc., as an extraordinary Saint.

p. 364

Ad 40: I heard Sr. A. Serafina tell that sometimes the Servant of God, while still living, to her Sisters who hesitated to undertake a journey for fear of bad weather, assured them saying that nothing would happen, and so it came about.

Et expleto examine super Interrogatoriis, interrogatus fuit R. Testis super Articulis, super quibus, Proc. fol. 1934v., respondit: As to the articles, having already set forth what is my concept about the holiness of the Servant of God, and not knowing, on the other hand, many particular facts of her life, I refer to what I have already said, and add that her intimate Sisters, such as Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega, Sr. A. Speranza, Sr. A. Serafina Foglia, Sr. A. Camilla Valentini, Sr. A. Amante La Barbera, and others had and have of her an esteem superior to that which I have; and this esteem is reflected in the same degree in the articles; yet I could not adduce, for the inferiority of my esteem, any particular reason apart from these. For example: When she was ill, she received Communion after midnight in the Chapel and then went to bed: this did not please me, since either she was in a condition to make Communion, or not; if she was not in a condition to make it, why make it?

Moreover, when she came to confess she was very brief, and did not seek spiritual pasture from the Confessor, as many other Sisters did, asking for it. I must add, however, that she accepted with reverence the words I said to her; indeed I will say further that sometimes, passing before me outside the Confessional, she took a sleeve of my habit and kissed it, or, if it was more convenient for her to kiss my cincture, she kissed that. But I did not like that not asking for pasture in the confessional.

Another, graver reason I heard from Sr. A. Serafina Foglia and from Sr. A. Michelina Negri, and from other Sisters whom I do not now recall: that the Servant of God did not treat too well those Superiors of Houses in which, when her relatives happened by, they had not shown themselves very solicitous for them; although those poor Superiors had not done more on account of the great poverty of the house; while on the contrary she showed herself very benevolent toward those Superiors who had shown themselves full of attentions for her relatives.

Likewise I did not like that Fr. Agostino Donadio had free access to this House: he came every morning to celebrate Mass in the Chapel (and when he could not, I supplied), and unfailingly every evening, an hour or an hour and a half before the Ave Maria, going up either to the Servant of God, or to the Secretariat, or to the garden, or to the kitchen, where into his wide sleeves he put something; all things forbidden to me. Fr. Agostino in the evening went to the Sacristy, and in the first times always waited for me for the service, which he however performed, I assisting him. Sometimes, however, it has happened to me that he did not wait for me.

State and profession: Religious in the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, Assistant General.

Quality of the witness: Eyewitness.

Length of acquaintance and its motivation: Entering religious life on 16 May 1876 at Piacenza, the witness was welcomed by the Servant of God herself; she maintained close contact with her in the various Houses to which she was assigned and, from 1894, lived in the Generalate House with the Foundress until her death.

Observations on the witness, on the scope and on the content of the deposition: The present testimony is of high value, for Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini shows herself a perfect connoisseur of the human and spiritual story of the Servant of God, and the information she reports offers exceptional material of proof. The imposing deposition, though of great interest in every part, has been broadly pruned, for obvious reasons.

The deposition can be divided into three parts:

1) Childhood, education of the Servant of God, marriage and conjugal life, education of her offspring, widowhood and charitable apostolate.

2) Birth and development of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, role of the Servant of God and principles that inspired her in the foundation; ample exposition of the facts and circumstances in which she exercised the office of Superior General; Apostolic Visitation and its motives; relations with the family.

3) Virtues in particular of the Servant of God, fame of holiness in life, supernatural gifts and fame of miracles.

The witness knew the Servant of God for fully 24 years (1876-1900); from 1884 to 1890 she was the first Provincial of Bolivia, the first mission of the Institute; Assistant General from 1895 to 1915; Pope Benedict XV charged her with governing the Institute as Vicar General from the death of Mother Carrega (February 1915) until the election of the new Superior General; from November 1915 to 1922 she was again Assistant General and from 1922 to 1930 she was Superior General. This biographical sketch of the witness suffices to establish the importance of her deposition, to explain its breadth and to demonstrate its credibility.

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 2003, testis respondit:

§ 575
General particulars of the witness.

My name is Anna Camilla Valentini, daughter of the late Giovanni Battista and Rosa Giudice. I was born at Oleggio, Province of Novara, on 21 April 1855. I was brought up in a Christian way in the family, and entered this Institute on 16 May 1876 at Piacenza. I was received by the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno. I took the habit on 19 June of the same year, and four months after the clothing I came to Rome, assigned to the Pontifical School of Our Lady of Repose, Parish of the Fornaci. I professed on the Feast of St. Anne in 1877, and almost three years I remained in that house, as Teacher. I was then sent to the civil hospital of Borgo San Donnino, where I remained four years, as Superior. I was sent afterward to America, to Bolivia, first as Superior of the Hospital of Sucre for three years, then I was named Provincial of the various houses of Bolivia, for two years, and was reconfirmed for another six years by the General Chapter, which however I did not complete, having been recalled to Italy and sent as Superior to Noci in Puglia, where I remained fifteen months; afterward I was sent as Superior to Bassano Veneto for four years; from there I was recalled to Rome and assigned to the Secretariat. A year later, that is in 1895, I was named by the General Chapter Assistant; and in this office every six years they have always reconfirmed me. After the death of Mother Carrega I was named Vicar General until the Chapter.

§ 576
Scope of acquaintance.

Ad 7: I came to know the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno at the very moment I entered the Institute, and she made on me the impression of a Saint.

My Confessor, who had guided me in the search for the Institute, had spoken to me of her very well. Not for having known her personally, but from information received from a friend of his, a Parish Priest at Nespolate di Novara, who was enthusiastic about her. To him my Confessor entrusted me and another Postulant to conduct us to Piacenza; and this Parish Priest, during the journey, spoke to us with such admiration of the Servant of God that nothing more could be said. At the end of his praises, from time to time he concluded: «And then you will see her, and at the mere sight of her you will call her a Saint».

The night of my arrival I passed sleepless, and I was resolved to leave the next morning, but having entered the Chapel for meditation, and having heard the Servant of God recite a point of the meditation on the Passion of Our Lord, from the accent with which she said it I was so penetrated that I remained in perfect calm and no longer thought of leaving. Note that I was already accustomed to meditation, and that point of meditation was no novelty to me, my own mother having accustomed me to this exercise.

Besides having known the Servant of God personally myself, besides having been in contact with her with the familiarity and confidence with which she honored me, which put me in a position to know many things of her life, many other persons gave me account of facts and things of hers.

Ad 8: I always keep a great affection for my venerated Mother Rosa Gattorno. I have esteem of her as a Saint and therefore nourish great devotion to her, and often commend myself to her. I pray for the good outcome of this Cause, but in it I have no involvement, I do nothing, and I willingly submit to the judgment of the Holy See.

§ 577
Family life, childhood and youth.

Ad 9: I know that the Servant of God was born in Genoa. Her mother was a holy woman; her father was a very honest merchant. Of her father we preserve some letters to her, which are truly edifying.

I do not remember who told me, but certainly I heard it from Sisters who were in our Community at Genoa, that the Servant of God, for her first Communion, prepared herself with mortifications and fasts, and that, so as not to be noticed by her parents that she was not eating, at table she deftly let the food fall into her lap instead of eating it, and then handed it to the maidservant to take to the poor. I think the maidservant herself, named Manin, told this to our Sisters at Genoa, and she was still alive, very old, when one of them told it to me. From the same source I learned that the little girl Rosa Gattorno grew ever more reserved and good, averse to amusements and without ambition; and also that she was a great lover of the poor, for whom she hid what was hers and especially food.

When she knew there was some sick person, not being able to go herself, because her family would not have permitted it, she being too small, she sent the help she could, and in this the good Manin kept her company. Of this Manin the Servant of God herself spoke to me with affection and good memory, saying that she gave her many good counsels and helped her in her works of charity and piety.

She also told me that in her father's house, as a young girl, she stayed up in the evening until late at night praying. (Her account gave me the impression that she did penances even at that time), but that she had to be very careful not to make any noise.

Proc. fol. 2011v.: Rarely did she speak to me of her own affairs, and when some word had slipped from her mouth that could put her in a good light, she showed herself alarmed and at once added: «But you will not tell it to anyone, will you?». And so she cut short her talk.

§ 578
Religious vocation.

She told me further that after making her first Communion she always felt the vocation to religious life, but that she could not speak of it in the family, where she would have found decided resistance, especially from her father. She continued therefore, as best she could, secretly and with the complicity of the good Manin, her holy works, until, her hand having been asked of her father by a cousin of hers, a certain Custo, he forced her into marriage, and I believe he forced her because she said to me, speaking of it: «I did nothing but obey». «Yet, — she added, — for this my not having followed the vocation I felt in my heart, I at once had the punishment deserved from the Lord, for the daughter I had at once was deaf-mute». Saying so, she wept.

The Servant of God then had two other children, of whom one died at once, the other in ninety-one. After the third child her husband fell ill and died of consumption; and it is incredible with how much love and how she assisted him, according to those of her own family, as I heard from her sister Elisa. She never moved from her husband's bedside. And she saw to it that he received the last Sacraments in time and well. She felt that loss greatly, as a Sister reported to me to whom she herself had told it (perhaps it was Mother Carrega who narrated it to me). But at the same time she felt the freedom regained to give herself more completely to works of charity and piety. She still felt the religious vocation strongly, but reflected at the same time that her first duty was to educate her children. She herself told me that her father, she having remained a widow and very young, that is at 27, wanted her at once back with him with her children.

Returned to her father's house, she was free in her good works and no longer needed to hide them, as before marriage, since from her parents she received no further remark.

§ 579
Practice of charity before the foundation.

Ad 16: The Servant of God went to the poor, to the sick at home, and every day, or almost, she went to the Pammatone Hospital, where she had (curious coincidence!) precisely assigned the Ward of St. Anne. In this Hospital a doctor, having appreciated her skill in caring, made use of her to send her to the sick to carry out those treatments that he himself had to do, and often made use of her also for cloistered nuns.

This she herself told me on the occasion (and it was occasions that made some personal story of hers come from her lips) when I, having a Sister in need of an operation, which she refused, accompanied her to the Servant of God, who, to comfort her and persuade her, brought forward the example of cloistered Nuns operated on and then dressed by her.

§ 580
President of the Daughters of Mary in Genoa.

The Archbishop of Genoa at that time made her President of various Congregations of Daughters of Mary.
