She gathered them and composed for them a rule, which she then submitted to the approval of the same Archbishop. Gathering the Daughters of Mary, she explained the rule to them. This I know from the Servant of God herself. These were the first Congregations of the Daughters of Mary in Genoa, which then spread everywhere.

In composing the said rule she felt herself more vividly impelled by her old religious vocation, to such a degree that its first points served as the basis of the first rules of our Institute. This I was told, I think, by Sr. Anna Celsa Speranza.

The Servant of God told me that her most beautiful hours in those times were those of the night: after putting her little children to bed, she made midnight and even one o'clock in prayer, the hours passing swiftly at the feet of her Crucifix.

§ 581
Called by the Crucifix.

Finally one day I came to learn from her that, while still a widow in her father's house, praying one night before a Crucifix, and feeling more than usual the impulse to follow her religious vocation, she said to her Crucifix: «But you see, O Lord, that I must also think of the children you yourself gave me». Behold, all of a sudden the Crucifix detaches itself from its Cross and falls into her arms.

The next day, in agreement with Manin, she has it nailed on by a blacksmith, but the following night again the Crucifix, while she prays, falls into her arms, and then finally she understands, and says to it: «Ah! so I have understood, O Jesus! The Cross is for me». And from then on she no longer tried to nail it.

When the Servant of God told me something personal of hers, she added: «You know that my affairs you must never tell to anyone». Yet this fact, after the death of the Servant of God, I have told to many persons.

The Archbishop, having come to Rome, spoke of this privileged soul to the Pope, as I learned from Consisters and from Fr. Agostino Donadio, and the Pope said to him: «Let me know her». The Archbishop, returned to Genoa, exhorted the Servant of God to go to the Pope and open her heart to him.

§ 582
Pius IX and the foundation.

Proc. fol. 2019v.: The Servant of God went to the Holy Father Pio Nono, who received her very well, having already been forewarned by the Archbishop of Genoa; she opened herself entirely to him, and received from him comfort and exhortation to put into act what God wanted of her, that is, to found the Institute.

For some days, having visited the holy places of Rome, she returned to Genoa to settle her children and all her affairs: the children she placed in a Boarding School.

And she confessed to me that she had suffered so much in leaving her mother, who could not detach herself from her and absolutely would not hear of it; in this she found her father finally more yielding, to such a degree that he said to her: «If you wish to leave the house you will have to trample on my body, and we shall see if you have the courage»; but she had the courage to step over him. She did not weep, but suffered greatly.

p. 372

§ 583
Beginning of the Foundation: religious habit.

Ad 20, Proc. fol. 2022v.: I do not know in what month she arrived at Piacenza, but certainly in 1866, and certainly on the Feast of the Immaculate Conception of that year the first clothing took place, while she herself was clothed on the Feast of St. Anne of the following year.

Pio Nono had advised her that the form of the habit she would give her Institute should be very simple and not catch the eye, also because of the times in which we live. And he showed himself very satisfied with our habit when the Servant of God presented her first Sisters to him on the occasion of the first foundation in Rome. This I heard from the Sisters and, if I am not mistaken, from the first Sisters themselves.

Our habit has always been the same from the beginning. The collar we wear the Servant of God already wore as a lay woman, a widow, as can be seen from a photograph of hers of that time. Only it must be noted that at the beginning in winter a little cloth jacket was worn instead of the scapular, but later, having to put on the gown in hospitals, as the doctors require, and the little jacket therefore sitting badly, the Servant of God then came to the decision that, if one is cold, one should put on an extra sweater, and leave off the little jacket.

I do not remember from which Sisters I heard that the model of our habit was given to her by St. Anne in a vision to the Servant of God, showing herself so clothed.

Speaking of the habit, it has come to my mind that the Servant of God, having become a widow, always dressed in black and very modestly. When she was married she dressed well because her husband wished it so; as I heard from the Sisters and from her family.

§ 584
Title of the Institute.

Proc. fol. 2027: The Servant of God would have wished her Institute to be called that of the Daughters of the Immaculate, as I heard from my Consisters, but I do not know how it was then called that of the Daughters of St. Anne. I have heard it said that the Sisters of St. Anne of Providence, having learned that another Institute was about to take the name of St. Anne, were alarmed, and spoke of it with their Cardinal Protector, who in turn spoke of it to the Pope, and then invited the Servant of God to go to the Pope, and she, when she was before him with some of her daughters, heard the Pope exclaim: «Oh, here are the Daughters of St. Anne», and so every controversy ended! The Cardinal Protector of the Sisters of St. Anne of Providence was also present.

p. 373

§ 585
Constitutions and their approval.

Ad 21: Our Constitutions are the work of the Servant of God.

When she was occupied with the Daughters of Mary, as she herself told me, her Archbishop charged her with making a rule, coming to an agreement with the prior of St. Sabina, Frassinetti; she, out of deference and for the very high esteem in which Frassinetti was held, had a rule given to her and brought it to the Archbishop, who however did not approve it and charged her again to make it herself. She set to work, but wishing to content herself with reducing Frassinetti's rule with variations. But she did not succeed, and found herself, without wishing it, to have made a work from the ground up. She worked before her Crucifix, and after praying much, and from Consisters I heard that during the time of this work she heard her Crucifix say: «This will serve you for another work». I know that she took this rule with her to Piacenza and applied it as the basis to her new Institute.

The definitive approval of the Constitutions was given by the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars, its Prefect being Cardinal Verga, Protector of our Institute, in 1892, on the occasion of the twenty-fifth anniversary of the Servant of God's religious clothing.

I have heard it said that she struggled so much and suffered so much to obtain such approval.

§ 586
Diligent discharge of the office of superior.

Ad 22: The Servant of God was always the head and the General of our Institute. But I believe always unwillingly, because in the last years I heard her say to us so many, many times: «But elect yourselves a General, and leave me a little in peace: I feel the need of rest. I will retire to pray, and with prayers I will obtain graces for you».

In this her office she perfectly fulfilled her duties, and if the successors have done anything, they have done it following her footsteps, and would feel scruple to depart by a jot from what she did. And we always say it among ourselves: «We shall never depart from what our Venerated Mother did».

I never knew that the Servant of God was lax in admitting Postulants into the Institute. I myself saw that in the beginning she sent away many. She did not compromise when she understood that, for one reason or another, the Postulant or the Novice was not made for her Institute. I myself, although animated by the best will, when I was a Novice, feared greatly that she would send me away, so rigid and strict did I see her in retaining her Daughters.

I remember a Novice, a certain Sr. Giusta, a Roman, presented by the Curate of the little Parish outside Porta Portese, whom the Servant of God did not see as suited to our Institute because of her unruly character, who, being an orphan, caused concern if she were sent away. The Curate himself earnestly begged the Servant of God not to send her away, for charity's sake, because of the great dangers to which she would remain exposed, having no one to take care of her. The Servant of God resigned herself to keeping her as long as she lived, but not as a Sister, nor sharing in the life of the Community.

§ 587
Prudence in the acceptance of postulants.

Proc. fol. 2036: The Servant of God received no Postulant unless she was recommended by the Parish Priests, and this always, since I remember. And this she most earnestly recommended to the Superiors on the occasion of her visits to the Houses. It was a continual recommendation of this. Not only that, but she also wanted them to take information from the Bishops about the Postulants.

An exception was made to this general rule, and it was for the pupils of our Schools; and even then she wanted a certain involvement of the Parish Priests when they applied to enter the Institute. And therefore without their certificates not even these are admitted.

§ 588
The novitiate at the beginning of the Institute: formation of the novices.

At the beginning of the Institute the Novitiate was not made regularly, and was not even fixed in the rule. But after it was fixed in the rules with the definitive approval, two whole years of Novitiate were always made by her, one in the Novitiate properly so called, and the other in the houses to which they were assigned. Until the definitive approval of the rules came, even the Cardinal Protectors, such as Alimonda and Verga (I heard them myself), said that in case of need, until the rules were definitively approved, the Novices could after six months be employed, sending them here and there according to need. But the Servant of God made use of this only in time of epidemic, needing to send persons for the assistance of the stricken. I heard from the Consisters that at the time of the Cholera of 1884 she went to the Novitiate of Piacenza to give a conference to make the Novices know the good they would do by offering themselves, and the great gain for Paradise. And even in these cases the Servant of God did not allow herself to have the Novitiate interrupted except with the consent of the Cardinal Protector. And so I found that the Servant of God did when I returned from America the first time, that is, in 1885. I could not determine the year in which she began to be so strict.

I remember, however, that when I went to America in 1882, with faculty to set up the Novitiate, the Servant of God told me to pay good attention that the Novitiate had to be a whole year in the Novitiate House.

Until we had the definitive approval of the Constitutions, those we had in hand determined three years of Novitiate simply, without determining that it had to be made in the proper Novitiate House. And so perhaps after a few months from the clothing the novices in the first times were sent here and there.

I received the letter from the Servant of God to make my Vows a year and a little more after my clothing, I having told her that I would have wished to postpone, because I did not yet feel prepared as I would have desired. I also wondered how this imposition could be reconciled with the rule of three years of Novitiate. I obeyed the Servant of God nevertheless, but with such pain that I fell ill, and when the Servant of God came to Rome, where I was, I asked her the explanation, and she answered me that the Pope, informed by her that the time of the Novitiate was set at three years, had answered her: «My daughter, one year is enough».

It is to be noted that the Servant of God, sending the Novices here and there to the Houses to work, soon came to know their spirit. And many during this trial were sent away, as indeed has always happened afterward too. And it is to have time to send away her Daughters that the Servant of God established that after the two years of Novitiate there should be ten more of probation.

That I noticed that the Servant of God asked the counsel of her Assistants, both for the clothing and for the profession, was in the year 1885, in the time that I stayed here on the return from America. And afterward she always continued to seek their counsel.

§ 589
Particular care of the novitiate: prudence in new foundations.

I do not know for certain whether before she acted on her own,

She was most jealous for the Novitiate, and was not content with the assistance of the Mistress, but took special care of it herself, and also of the Postulancy. In my time she often went to give conferences. She was tireless in her care of the Novitiate.

The Servant of God, when she had to make a foundation, first went to the place herself, after having already dealt by letters. She assured herself in person of the dwelling of the Sisters, that it be secluded, and of all things as agreed, and only then sent the Sisters. Her foundations were always made following an invitation.

The Servant of God, as I said, having arrived at Piacenza, gave herself to the care of the sick at home, and then began to gather little orphans, and in the winter of 1878-79 I myself saw her many times (and I know she did it all winter) giving soup and bread to the poor. I myself cannot even conceive how she could have done it.

From the beginning the Servant of God began to have many requests from her Sisters, and the Lord also sent her many vocations, so that the clothings were quite numerous. It was almost ten years since the Institute had begun, and at my entrance I was already the two hundred and fortieth Sister.

I believe the first house was the hospital of Cento.

At the death of the Servant of God our Institute counted about three hundred houses, including those of Africa, America, France and Spain. In America we were already in Bolivia, Brazil, Peru and Chile.

§ 590
Zeal and vigilance for observance in visits to communities.

Proc. fol. 2043v.: The Servant of God always visited her houses with the greatest zeal and diligence, until illness absolutely prevented her. The last journey she made to Sicily was in 1898, which however she could not complete, because of failing health, going personally everywhere; yet she wished first to see all the Sisters, and had them come to her, and then the Superiors, whom she then gathered in Spiritual Exercises. In the same year, returned to Rome, after Naples, where she visited some house, she returned to Piacenza and from there again to visit the houses.

In 1899 I too accompanied her on the visit to the three Houses of Ovada (I had accompanied her also on the journeys of 1898); and then she went to Sestri Ponente, then to Sampierdarena and to Genoa, where, the illness which had been growing ever more becoming accentuated, she returned to Rome, accompanied also by the attending physician.

p. 377

As soon as she arrived at a House, as also before departing (as we have by rule), she went to the Chapel or Church of the Sisters, where the Superiors had the Priest ready and the Altar already lit to celebrate, if it was morning, or to give Benediction with the Blessed Sacrament, if at another hour. Then the Servant of God shut herself in her room, after having told the Sisters that if any had something to say, she should freely go and say it to her. There she received all; indeed she wished to see them all one by one. But if there was a sick one, before hearing the other Sisters she went to visit her; and how many received health!

§ 591
Motherly gentleness in dealing with the religious.

Privately she gave to each the counsels they asked of her, the admonitions, the comforts according to the case, always with much gentleness, for it may be said that she was gentleness personified; and after hearing them all, including the Superior, she gathered them all and gave them a conference on charity, on the conduct to be kept in Community, tolerating one another and bearing with each other with patience; on the conduct to be kept with outsiders, and above all in hospitals, with the doctors, at the bedside of the sick, and for the schools on the practical way of educating girls, and oh! how long she dwelt on this point.

§ 592
Spiritual exercises desired by the foundress.

To consolidate her Sisters in the practical way of educating youth in a Christian manner, especially in the first years of the Institute, she gathered them all in Spiritual Exercises given expressly for them: she did the same for the nurses, and the same for the Superiors. These Spiritual Exercises, however, she did not want to dispense the Sisters from the spiritual Exercises of the Community. And where there were difficulties in making the Exercises, she taught the Provincial Superiors the way to satisfy this requirement; and to encourage the Provincials she used to say: «Where the Exercises are made every year, the Sisters will all become Saints». When in a House they were about to begin the Exercises, the blessing of the Servant of God was asked. How pleased she was then, and what telegrams she sent! She then had followed such beautiful letters that they made us fall ever more in love with the love of God.

Either before or after the visit to the Houses she went to the Diocesan Bishop to hear his advice and information. She admonished the Provincials not to visit any house without first notifying the Bishop, and where there was no Bishop, the Parish Priest or the Archpriest.

p. 378

§ 593
Corrections and distribution of offices.

If she found some abuse in a House, she went to the bottom of it; if she knew that a Sister was not suited for that House, or was in danger there, she cut short and took her away. In the distribution of offices, as far as I could understand, she had no human respect and did not let herself be led by ulterior motives. First of all she prayed much for this purpose. She told me that she always did so, and insistently inculcated it also on us Superiors, that we should make prayers before taking any decision. Even for a simple letter she suggested we wait before writing it: «Go to Jesus in the Blessed Sacrament, and after praying, write». Once she said to me: «And after writing it, sleep on it before sending it».

§ 594
Report of a presumed miracle.

Proc. fol. 2054: She had me put in a room of the guest quarters so as not to go up to the dormitories of the Community, and entrusted me to the care of the infirmarian Sr. A. Silvestrina, now deceased, whose surname I do not remember. But she did not send for any doctor, did not have ice provided for me, nor any other special care. I meanwhile suffered, and for that night and for some fifteen more nights I did not sleep at all because of the pains of my leg, and also from the thought of the sorrow my parents would feel, who certainly would not have wanted me to go to America. The Servant of God herself, however, took charge of keeping up the correspondence with them in this circumstance, and knew how to resign them. She came to see me several times a day, to ask how I was, but without any concern, although the ailment did not recede and indeed the progress of the threat of gangrene appeared manifest, because it kept on suppurating though it did not spread. One day she told me that she had promised mine to have my photograph taken to send to them as a keepsake. Note well that in those days photographs were not taken individually of any Sister, but only collectively of those who left for America. I made the Servant of God reflect that mine would be shocked to see me suffering, because indeed the sufferings of the leg had made me decline in appearance, but the Servant of God said to me: «Oh, as to that, you will be smiling, and you will see that you will not appear to be suffering».

After some fifteen days or so from my arrival at Piacenza, one morning, although my foot was still swollen so as to have no shape and was still black, the Servant of God comes to me a little before the hour when I usually got up, and says to me: «As I promised yours to have your photograph taken, today you will have it taken. Get up and go to the photographer». I had imagined until then that she had called the photographer to the house, and therefore I observed to the Mother that it would be impossible to put my shoe on, and not even to rest my foot on the ground. But she, for all answer, says to me: «Get up and make the obedience», and to the infirmarian: «Take the shoe and put it on her». What was the surprise of mine and of the infirmarian when, while she was putting the shoe on me, the foot went down and returned to its normal state, and the black also disappeared, and every other trace, as I then saw, and all the swelling of the leg also disappeared. I walked at once without any difficulty and without any pain, and went out freely with the infirmarian, and went to the photographer about ten o'clock, and then continued to walk with the infirmarian all over Piacenza until two in the afternoon, the infirmarian having to make various purchases. As soon as I realized the miracle, the infirmarian and I were moved; and I wanted to kiss the hand of my Mother out of gratitude, saying to her: «Is it you who made this miracle for me?». But she, who until the last years of her life never let her hand be kissed, fending me off answered me: «It was not I who did it for you, you know, but it was the Holy Mother. Now do you believe that it is the Lord who wants you in America?». And to me and to the infirmarian: «Do not tell anyone what has happened».

When the Servant of God had to choose some Sister for a delicate post, also because of contact with outsiders, she gathered us Assistants and the Secretary in council and said to us: «Help me!», and, on our proposals of persons, she chose. So also for the requests of some Provincial who desired to change personnel in this or that House, and so for the profession and assignment of the Novices.

§ 595
She treated the sisters with great charity.

Ad 23: The Servant of God, as to the treatment of her Sisters, wanted it to be that of the Generalate House, and this was her invariable order to all the Superiors; and this she wrote also in the Circulars. She did not permit that any Sister lack anything. If any had need, by medical prescription, of special food, she wanted it to be supplied. If some house lacked the means, she said to the Superior: «Where you do not reach, I reach, but I want the Sisters to be well treated». When she visited the Houses, and noticed that some Superior was a bit tight-fisted, and that therefore something was lacking to the Sisters, she admonished her, gave her counsels, and made her understand that when the Sister is well treated she is happier, works willingly and better.

§ 596
Contribution of the communities to the generalate house.

Proc. fol. 2061v.: What was left over to the various Houses she required to come to the Generalate House; and therefore in the visits, when she found useless expenses in the accounts, then she warned. I never heard that any Superior, to make a good showing before the Servant of God, skimped the treatment of the Sisters, and thus send a larger surplus to the Generalate House. I know that sometimes some Superior allowed herself to send something to poor relatives, or to give particular alms without permission of the Servant of God; but she, as soon as she came to know it, admonished the Superior. I myself heard her say to a Superior who had done so: «Oh! my daughter, if you had told me, I would have given you the money for your relatives». For in fact she used to help the poor relatives of the Sisters.

She did not require of a House more than it could reasonably give. There were those which she, on the contrary, had to help. To me myself she said one day, when in the last year I was Superior at the Fornaci: «What do you want to give me, you who do not have enough for yourself?»; and once, having made some savings, I wanted to bring it myself to the Mother; but she would not even receive it, and said to me: «Where did you steal it? It is not possible that you could have saved it!». And it was really so, for that saving had not come from the ordinary resources, but from some gift and little jobs done and alms.

To some Superior, however, who did send a surplus but not all that she could have sent, the Mother gave the opportune warning. In short, she required the superfluous and did not want and did not permit that the Sisters lack anything.

§ 597
She did not permit that the sisters lack anything.

Likewise I never heard, I never noticed, that the Servant of God insisted with the Superiors to have a surplus that went beyond the superfluous. Indeed I remember that when the general summary of accounts was sent to her, if she saw that little had been spent on food, she asked the Superiors for an account of this little. And these, according to the case, if they had received gifts of wheat or other, justified themselves.

For the sick Sisters, then, I cannot say how great was her solicitude. If they were in her house, she visited them continually. To the Superiors she said that a sick person in the house draws the blessings of the Lord; she often wanted news of them and always took an interest.

§ 598
The Servant of God and her relationship with her deaf-mute daughter.

Ad 24, Proc. fol. 2063v.: The Servant of God, as I said, had a deaf-mute daughter, named Carlotta, whom, as I heard, she kept several years in an Institute at Milan, from which she was obliged to take her back, having learned that secretly she was about to arrange a marriage with another deaf-mute. The Servant of God would indeed have desired that her daughter become a Sister and remain unmarried, as I learned from her herself, and she took her therefore here and there to visit monasteries to see whether there was one she liked, but in vain. Carlotta always said that she liked the world. I do not know then how the marriage with Count Gaspare Barbiellini came about. I know that the Mother sent Carlotta to Genoa to her brothers and there the marriage was celebrated.

Count Barbiellini showed himself very Catholic and practicing; and I remember that even during the time when he was maintaining with us, after the death of our Mother, an unjust lawsuit, he did not fail to receive Communion every Sunday. He always brought the children to Church, at home he never omitted the rosary any day. Toward his mother-in-law he showed himself respectful in the first years.

§ 599
She entrusted the administration of Gargatano to her brother and son-in-law.

About 1885-86 the Institute received the estate of Gargatano in Piacenza, and the Servant of God, feeling the need to put a trustworthy person there to administer it, entrusted it to her brother Francesco, who held it in administration for three years, and afterward entrusted it to her son-in-law. Here he began to profit, unlike Francesco, who showed perfect honesty, as appeared evidently from his accounts. This profiting of Barbiellini did not appear in the first years, because then he went slowly, but afterward he had no more shame. The Servant of God began first by calling him to his duty; Barbiellini tried to present one thing for another, defending himself, but in the end the Mother took away his power of attorney, and this I think happened in 1894. Then pandemonium broke loose.

I note here that the estate of Gargatano was left by the Counts Caracciolo to the Institute for the sole exclusive purpose of an infirmary for our sick Sisters; and this many know. And this very thing Mother Speranza went to answer to the Sacred Congregation, having been asked by it, that is, in a memorial.

His power of attorney having been taken away, Count Barbiellini brought to our House at Piacenza his wife and children, saying to the Servant of God: «Keep your daughter and the grandchildren». I was present. The Servant of God had Lawyer Gian Carlo Bonfiglio come from Genoa to deal with the son-in-law. And so Barbiellini was forced to withdraw his family from our House. We noticed, however, that on that occasion a comedy was being played: because Carlotta, at that time when the Mother and the Sisters were in Church, wrote little notes, and then at the window waited for her husband and from the window threw them to him. Naturally some Sister in the House was about, and so she was caught. I too personally formed this idea of a comedy, because I came upon some little note that Carlotta left under some papers on her writing desk, when she was surprised by the Mother, and I read two or three words of one.

§ 600
Prudence of the Servant of God toward her son-in-law.

Proc. fol. 2069: Moreover I myself saw Carlotta throw the little notes to her husband from the window. So I put the Servant of God on her guard that it was a comedy, and it was then that she called Lawyer Bonfiglio. I must note that she informed of everything the Cardinal Protector of that time, and he encouraged her to hold firm in the refusal of the power of attorney to her son-in-law, and approved the calling of the said lawyer. All this I know because I was present.

I remember that, we being present, the Servant of God said thus to Lawyer Bonfiglio: «For charity's sake, I entrust myself to you, do things well, because you must be the defender of my Sisters after my death». And the Institute called the same Lawyer to defend our Cause, after the death of the Mother, against Barbiellini, and he is always our Lawyer.

After the refusal of the power of attorney and after Barbiellini had taken back his wife and children, he did not stay quiet; and then, with the counsel of the Cardinal Protector, the Servant of God gave him a sum that I could not determine. The Servant of God naturally suffered much. Barbiellini had been capable even, after he had received the money for the payments, of claiming to receive other money, having had the receipts made out in his name. And this was the reason why the Cardinal advised, for peace's sake, to give him a sum. The Servant of God gave money to the Administrator of the estate, and this on the advice of the Generalate Council. After these events the Servant of God gave him no further assignment.

Before Count Gaspare Barbiellini was dismissed, his brother, Count Edoardo, entered as agent of our House of Rome, who also did his own tricks, and the Servant of God was obliged to dismiss him too in the last years of her life; and for him too she suffered greatly.

Count Edoardo, having always received the money for the payments, made false receipts in the name of the firms supplying the Mother House for the sum of about ten thousand lire. But one fine day these firms notified the Servant of God, who then saw the grave swindle and then, without more ado, put the swindler out the door, notwithstanding his insistent entreaties to remain. Yet she forgave him.

I remember that Carlotta sometimes came to her Mother to show her, weeping, the bruises from the blows received from her husband. The Servant of God naturally suffered also for this, for that poor and excellent creature.

§ 601
Difficulties arising from the contiguity of the Gattorno dwelling and the convent.

Both here in Rome and at Piacenza Barbiellini and family lived in a house adjoining ours. The one at Piacenza was their property with an attached garden, and there was communication between the two gardens of the two Houses. This communication was closed before the Apostolic Visitation by the Servant of God herself, on the Bishop's remarks; not because he saw any harm in it, but to silence the malicious.

The House in Rome was the property of Barbiellini for one floor, and for the other two of the brothers of the Servant of God. This had no communication with our House.

I have heard from the Sisters that the construction of this Generalate House in Rome was imposed on the Servant of God by the Holy Father Leo through the Cardinal Protector. She, however, did not have a cent. And I heard it told by the present Mother General and by the late M. Anna Benedetta Carrega that she then turned to her two brothers, who were bankers or belonged to a bank, that they might help her, and to her brother Federico, who said to her: «To put yourself into such an enterprise you too will have to have something, and then we will help you», she showed her only capital at that moment, which was thirty cents. The Servant of God, however, did not lose heart, and in the end induced her brothers to help her, and they let her have a large sum, which Mother Carrega afterward finished paying.

The relatives of the Servant of God often came to the house: the daughter came to say good day to the Mother, and went away. They were not, however, to come while the Servant of God was giving work to her Secretaries, because she would not have received them for any reason. They did not come every day, however; and the daughter, if she returned in the afternoon sometimes, it was to show the Mother the bruises made by Gaspare, or for some quarrel in the house. So at least most of the times.

The grandchildren came to the house because they went to school, and Sr. Giuseppina Tornatore was their teacher. They came, however, only when Sr. Giuseppina could not go to their house on account of indisposition.

Sometimes the Servant of God did not want them in the house, and then she said to the Sister: «It is better that you go to their house». And sometimes, Sr. Giuseppina being ill, I went. Coming to the house, however, they could not wander about the house. They went up by the stairs of the porter's lodge, and in a room of this the teacher gave lessons. Sometimes, naturally, they ran off to greet their grandmother. If the Servant of God allowed them to go to the garden, always accompanied by the teacher, she did not want them to go when there were Sisters. She did not permit them to go to the refectory, nor to the kitchen, and I remember that once when the Servant of God was at the second table, her little granddaughter Annina, crying for I know not what, received a scolding from her, and she sent her away.

I never saw the relatives even in conversation with the Servant of God at the second table, neither here nor at Piacenza. I went sometimes to the first table, sometimes to the second, according to my occupations.

§ 602
The religious and the relatives of the Servant of God.

Proc. fol. 2078: I never knew, nor saw, that the relatives of the Servant of God ever went to the kitchen to ask for or take things. If some sweet was made, naturally we Sisters sometimes had part of it sent to the Mother's family, without her knowing anything; and then afterward we told her, and sometimes she approved, sometimes not.

It must be noted that when these little gifts were destined, as I said above, they were sent to our porter's lodge, whence the Barbiellini came to fetch them. The same may be said if baskets of fruit were given to us.

Sometimes some Superior came from outside who had known Carlotta since childhood, and how could she excuse herself from bringing something also for the daughter of the Servant of God? So I too did when I came from outside. But when I arrived, I said to the Servant of God: «These things, Mother, I had destined for Carlotta, if you permit».

I never noticed, I never knew, that servants of the Barbiellini ever slept in our House. And since the time I have been near the Mother, that is from 1894 onward, I should surely have noticed, had it happened.

I know that Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega greatly benefited the Barbiellini family out of her own. When Carlotta came to her Mother weeping, perhaps prompted by her husband, as we understood, and the mother could not or would not satisfy her in what she asked, Carrega was moved, and to relieve the Servant of God of distress and to please the daughter she herself disbursed money. But Mother Carrega provided herself with the permission of the Cardinal Protector, as I learned from her herself; and I also heard Cardinal Verga, Protector of our Institute, say to her: «With the due permissions you can do what you like with the money».

I know that the Servant of God sometimes gave strong scoldings to Carrega for these largesses; and said to her: «You get them used to it badly: they will form the persuasion that everything must come from here». I heard the Servant of God answer her daughter who asked her for money: «I have nothing: what there is belongs all to the Institute».

Besides Mother Carrega, the Princess of Fitalia also and other persons, among whom I recall the Princes Berligeri of Cotrone, were generous toward the Servant of God in money, that she might use it for her own family. I myself heard the Servant of God say to us: «You see that I give, but if I give something to my daughter, I give what I can give and which is not the Institute's».

As to her son Alessandro, he indeed caused his mother trouble for some time, either because he did not want to study, or because he then wished to go to America, and there without guidance he remained some time, and then returned poorer than before; yet he gave no special annoyance to his mother on account of money. I must note that when the Servant of God devoted herself to the work of the Institute, she entrusted the administration of the patrimony of her two sons to a certain D. Accinelli, a good Priest of Genoa, who afterward, in giving money to Alessandro, regulated himself by the Mother's counsel.

The brother of the Servant of God, Federico, never refused to help his sister when she asked him, although she did not spare him reproaches when she knew of some anticlerical act of his. And I myself witnessed some philippic she made him, even of an hour, and he listened to her without keeping silent.

When the brothers were in Rome, they came to see her every eight or fifteen days; if Federico, however, had received a philippic, he stayed away for some months. Both brothers had a veneration for the Servant of God.

§ 603
Testament of the Servant of God in favor of the Institute.

Proc. fol. 2086: As to the will, the Servant of God did not favor her grandchildren at the expense of the Institute, but left everything in full order. After her death the son-in-law presented a signature of the Servant of God on a piece of paper without date. But Mgr. Serafini, Apostolic Visitor, when he saw it, warned Barbiellini to withdraw it absolutely, otherwise he would have him arrested. And Lawyer Carlo Santucci, Barbiellini's defender, when he saw that paper, abandoned the Cause. On that paper Barbiellini had written that the Servant of God owed him fifty thousand lire. The Servant of God never had even a chair in her own name.

§ 604
Origin and motive of the Apostolic Visitation.

Ad 25: As to the Apostolic Visitation, with which Mgr. Domenico Serafini, now Cardinal, was charged, I have heard it said that it was originated by denunciations of Count Barbiellini. I was present at Piacenza when Mgr. Serafini presented himself to begin the visitation. In this first meeting of the Visitor with the Servant of God I recall nothing special, except that the Servant of God was much impressed when she learned the purpose of that presenting of Mgr. Serafini, and invited him into the parlor that he might tell her what he had to do. I believe that Mother A. Benedetta Carrega also remained present at that conversation, because she was not accustomed ever to remain alone with outsiders.

§ 605
The book of the Servant of God «Labors and Consolations of a Soul».

Mother A. Benedetta Carrega and other Sisters told me that Barbiellini, having managed to filch a book written by the Servant of God, which bore the title «Labors and Consolations of a Soul», took it to the Sacred Congregation of Bishops and Regulars that it might provide. The Servant of God, when she remained in the parlor with Mgr. Serafini, saw him present to her the said book of hers, saying to her, as she herself told us immediately afterward: «This was written by you». She, for all answer, shrugged her shoulders, lacking the strength to say: «Yes, it was I». She wanted to speak but could not. She felt herself falling, and after shrugging her shoulders two or three times, there came from her mouth: «It was the Princess of Fitalia who had it printed». However, since that copy which Mgr. Serafini had presented was not of the latest, but only of the first, and therefore smaller, and with ecclesiastical approval only, she sent for the latest edition, which is a much larger and more complete volume, and with the approval not only of the Ecclesiastical authority, but also with a letter of His Eminence Guarino, Archbishop of Messina, and with a further letter of commendation from the Confaloniere of Florence. And handing this volume to Mgr. Serafini, she said to him: «Here it is, it is this one». And then, still alarmed and impressed, the Servant of God said to the Visitor: «Do you assure me that there is nothing against the faith?». And the Visitor: «No, against the faith there is absolutely nothing; but only some exaggeration; yet withdraw all the copies given to your Sisters, not those given to outsiders».

At the handing over of this copy I was present. The Servant of God that very day wrote everywhere for the withdrawal of that book, and that it be sent to His Eminence Verga, Protector of the Institute, then Major Penitentiary. This happened in July 1898.

Here is the history of this book. We Sisters, and also the Princess of Fitalia, often urged the Servant of God to write something about the Institute, about its origins, etc., because we were persuaded that this would greatly benefit, for the history of the Institute, those who would survive afterward. She, however, always demurred, saying she was averse to writing, that it would profit nothing. I also heard tell from the first Sisters and from the late Mrs. Onorata Colli that the first Secretary of the Servant of God, Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino, had written much on the origins of the Institute, but because in this writing there was much talk of the Mother, she, having found it, gave it at once to the flames. From this one understands how averse she was to having herself talked about. Among the Sisters from whom I heard this fact told is the living Sr. A. Beatrice Meriggi, Vice-Superior of the Mother House of Piacenza.

In the end the Servant of God, after repeated urging from us and from the Princess of Fitalia, was induced to write something in the night hours. When then the said Princess came to Rome, most eager to have her writing, the Servant of God handed her the part ready, and when she returned to Rome, the Princess, in returning to the Servant of God the part she had already read, received the following part. After reading various parts, the Princess showed herself enthusiastic, and begged the Servant of God to let her have it printed, for she would see to the expenses; and, permission having been obtained after a little hesitation (permission which the Servant of God granted in the persuasion that no one would understand anything, as she herself told us, and after having warned the Princess that it was necessary to secure Ecclesiastical approval), she had five hundred copies printed. It was then a little booklet which, as far as I know, was not distributed even to the Sisters, to whom she distributed the second edition, much enlarged and with the letters I spoke of above.

When the Servant of God said to us that no one would ever understand anything, we said to her that we understood (and I in reality understood everything), and she then answered us: «You yes, you will understand something, because you are near me; for the rest, if it can do you good, I thank God, and am very glad».

Certainly for the Sisters who did not come close to the Servant of God, that book is somewhat obscure, because she speaks under symbols.

With regard to the withdrawal of this book I recall that, some house having shown a little difficulty in returning it, because they did not want to be deprived of that book of their Mother, a book that helped them so much in spirit, she insisted on its withdrawal, saying that it needed corrections.

I never had the order, nor do I know that it was ever given, although I was then in the Secretariat, to warn the various Houses where the Visitor would go, nor to suggest anything for the hearings of the Visitor himself.

The Servant of God never hindered the Apostolic Visitation in any way and said: «The work is the Lord's, he will see to defending it». I myself was present when the Visitor, coming to her, paid her compliments on the Houses he had visited. From these praises she felt much encouraged, and said to us: «It is useless; the Work is the Lord's». I was present when she sometimes said to the Visitor: «Excellency, if you need money, tell me».

The word of the Visitor was for her a commandment of God. As far as I know, however, the Visitor never proposed things of great importance. The Servant of God did not have the comfort of seeing the triumph in this Apostolic Visitation, which lasted two or three years still after her death. I say triumph because the report made by Mgr. Serafini was completely in favor of the Institute, as is attested by the letter of commendation received by the Institute from His Eminence the Protector Cardinal Rampolla.

§ 606
Living faith of the Servant of God.

Ad 27, Proc. fol. 2095: The Servant of God possessed and exercised the Theological virtues, the Cardinal ones, those of the religious vows, and all the other related ones, such as Humility, patience, etc.

The Servant of God used to say that God had set Faith for her in diamond, so deep and living did she feel it in her heart. I heard her say many times that she would be ready to give her blood for the faith.

When the Sisters left for the Missions (twice I left myself, and other times I was present when the Servant of God spoke to those who were leaving), one had to hear how her discourses were inflamed by faith. «You go to foreign lands, wild, barbarous, without religion, not knowing what you will meet. There may be those who will tempt you about our Religion, but the true one is only one, and this is ours. Let it never be that instead of converting you let yourselves be perverted. Be strong, never depart from the Crucifix: I give it to you as a pledge. In anguish, in difficulties, do not pour yourselves out so much with this one and that one, but with your Crucifix». She gave us practical counsels for the journey, until we should reach our House, where we would be a little safer. «If you find yourselves in some revolution, she added, and are tempted in the faith, give your life too»; and here she made us eager for martyrdom, so much as to leave regret at not having found it. She did not put before us comforts, successes, triumphs, but put before us that we had to suffer, that we had to endure, yet at the same time pointing out the great rewards to be obtained from Jesus.

In her discourses and in all her letters she could never fail to recall her Crucifix, and she invariably closed them «in my Crucifix».

When I asked her counsel in some difficulty, she gave it to me, but at the same time added: «Go, run to your Crucifix, and if you have faith you will infallibly obtain».

§ 607
Apostolic spirit.

She was enrolled in the work of the Propagation of the Faith. By association of ideas I recall that she was enrolled in the Third Order of St. Francis, and in the little scapular of the Immaculate. She recommended to us very much to pray for the propagation of the faith, and in the prayer manual of the Institute she wished some for the propagation of the faith to be inserted, which we recite every day.

From the age of fifteen she began to instruct the girls of the Parish in the Catechism, as she herself told us, and added that she felt so much satisfaction when, going on summer holiday with her family, in catechizing not only the young but also the old, and that therefore she gathered as many as she could to instruct them.

I having written to her from America that the poor Indians were baptized, yes, but that they knew nothing else beyond being baptized, the Servant of God answered me: «Do not neglect them, you know. When they come to the Hospital and are ill in their beds, assign a Sister to give them an hour of Catechism a day». And this for every ward. When we wrote to her the good results of our work, oh how pleased she was, and she wrote us letters from which all her joy shone through.

§ 608
Eucharistic life.

Proc. fol. 2128: Since the Servant of God became a religious, she herself told us when we were together, she never left off daily Communion, except one single time through obedience; and I have heard it said by some Sister that this obedience she rendered to Mr. Tornatore, Priest of the Mission.

I have heard it said that even before being a Religious she always made it. After her first Communion, she herself told me, she felt drawn in a particular way toward that act; and therefore she made it often even at that childish age. Finding herself on a journey, as a Religious, she remained fasting just to be able to make Communion. In the last years, being ill with her heart, and feeling herself therefore sometimes faint, the Cardinal Protector, at the request of the Servant of God, to whom in turn it had been suggested by us, obtained for her the privilege of being able to take something even before Communion. The Confessor also exerted himself for this, as I seem to be certain.

Of this privilege, then, she made use in extreme necessities, when she really could not do without it, and then she took a little cup of coffee, always without sugar, and sometimes a cup of chamomile.

§ 609
She confessed frequently.

As far as I saw, she was not long in Confession, and that she was brief was commonly said among us Sisters. Sometimes it could last a quarter of an hour, sometimes half an hour, and sometimes even less. Half an hour, it seems to me one cannot say. She did not like long confessions, as she told us, because, according to her, ordinarily long confessions are not well made. «Long confessions are proper to scrupulous souls, and not so ready to obey», she said. «When the Confessor, she added, says to be at peace about something, one must not return to it». «The confession well made, — she told us, — must be sincere, frank and brief» and she went into particulars. After confession we saw that sometimes she remained long in prayer, but at other times it was brief, perhaps because other duties of her office required her. In the Novitiate she taught us the way of making the thanksgiving.

The Servant of God was very devoted to the Most Holy Trinity, in whose honor she composed three short prayers, which we had printed on the back of her image, and she exhorted us too to such devotion.

Proc. fol. 2201: Before going further, I must rectify one thing.

Speaking of the privileges granted by Pio Nono to the Servant of God, I had said that the privilege of the three Masses at midnight of Holy Christmas had been granted to her in 1866, whereas instead the privilege of one Mass was granted in 1871, and of the other two in 1874.

And now, proceeding with the matter I began to narrate in the last session, I shall say that before leaving for America, however, I went to say goodbye to mine, but I wished to hurry so as to be, on my return, with the Mother on Good Friday. I therefore arranged so that I managed to return here on Holy Thursday. I found the Mother making the visit to the Holy Sepulchre. Toward evening she shut herself in her room, from which, as usual, she would not come out until the morning of Holy Saturday.

On Good Friday, she being shut in, no one dared to approach even the door. But about three and half past three in the afternoon, I dared and stayed listening behind the door. Having put my hand on the handle, to my surprise I found it open and went in.

It must be noted that, since I was to leave, the Mother showed herself tender toward me, knowing that I was making a sacrifice, and I therefore supposed that she would not reprimand me for my indiscretion, and even reprimanded, it would have mattered nothing to me. I found the Servant of God on the bed, half dressed, but more dead than alive.

§ 610
The phenomenon of the stigmata.

The Servant of God never let anyone touch her, not even the doctor to feel her pulse, except in the last years; by me, however, because of my experience acquired in hospitals, she let herself be touched, and even sometimes invited me to feel her pulse to see whether she had a fever, but she wanted me to do it with only two fingers. Taking advantage, therefore, of the permission and invitation had other times, the first thing I did on seeing her thus in bed was to take her hand and touch her pulse. But, good God! an atrocious pain was communicated to me in my whole right arm. Believing that it was from some mishap taken at the moment, I tried with my left hand, but the pain was communicated equally to the left arm, to such a degree that I had to sit down because I could not bear it. The Servant of God, in the act of my touching her with my left hand, said to me: «Oh, do you want to be crucified too?». And I: «But what is the matter with you?». «Now I understand what the Sisters have always told me, I believe by supposition, that you suffered all the pains of the Passion on this day in company with Our Lord. Ah, then it is true?». And she: «You have surprised me, and since you have surprised me, woe to you if you speak. Yes, since last evening I began to suffer with Our Lord all the pains of his Passion, successively, one by one». And then I asked her: «Ah, then you have the stigmata?». «Yes», she answered me. And I again: «All the stigmata, or some?». «All», she answered me again. And I resumed also: «For how long? Did you have them visible or invisible?». And she answered me: «At first I had them visible, I was still in the world, and they were a great encumbrance to me, since I went to assist the sick, and before the persons to whom I had to present myself; but I prayed my Crucifix to make them invisible for me». She said twenty-eight years, but I could not now say whether it was twenty-eight years that she had had the stigmata or whether she had received them at the age of twenty-eight. That day and also other times I saw all red on her forehead the marks of the pains of the crowning with thorns, and once in particular, seeing her with these red points, I said to her: «But your headache which you complain of today, I understand well what it is!». But she made a sign to me with her finger on her lips to be silent. Sr. A. Amante La Barbera was present, who understood nothing. The Servant of God tried to hide these red points, keeping the veil down over her forehead, but I had already seen and noticed them.

On Holy Saturday, when she came out of her room, together with her face of Paradise it was seen and noticed by all the Sisters that her body was worn out; yet she was full of activity, as if she wished to compensate herself for the rest reserved on Good Friday.

On Easter Monday (in Albis), on leaving for America, she made me promise secrecy once more, saying to me: «Since my Jesus has done you this grace, you must swear to me that you will never speak of it». And so I did. When, however, I returned definitively from America, she never again entered into this subject, and if I entered into it she knew promptly how to divert it, and even then she made me promise again not to speak of it. And I was never again able to approach her with that familiarity with which she had favored me in the intervals, when, returned from America, I stayed with her. Indeed I noticed that she tried to keep me away from her precisely on those days in which she suffered most, so that I might notice less.

§ 611
Hope: the soul always turned to heaven.

Proc. fol. 2261v.: The Servant of God, as to Hope, I can attest that she always had her soul turned to Heaven. «At all costs, — she used to say, — I want to go to Paradise and drag there all my daughters», as I myself heard. Whether she admonished us or comforted us, her words were always seasoned with the hope of the eternal goods that await us.

Always, however, her hope had as foundation, as her words showed, the merits of Our Lord.

She counted the goods of this earth for nothing, and nothing either the protection of men. «See, — she told us, — as long as things go well with us, everyone crowds around you, and when they go badly, everyone abandons us and leaves us alone. Learn from this never to put trust in men».

If some providence of money came, she was glad, because she saw the way to enlarge the work of the Lord. She handled much money, but never had a penny in reserve. And she never ran after pecuniary dowries of Sisters.

I never knew that she urged her Sisters to give to the Institute more than the regulation thousand lire of dowry.

Proc. fol. 2282: As she felt hope, so also she sought to infuse it in her Sisters, both by speaking and by writing.

And how many times she taught me to write in her name, infusing Hope! And to make sure whether I had interpreted her thought well, in writing to Sisters who had much need of comfort, and whether I had been effective enough, she had them all brought to her desk, and had the courage to read them all.

§ 612
Perfect charity toward God.

As to Charity, I must say that the Servant of God seemed to me perfect in everything, whether this was because of the great affection I bore her or because of reality. I never discerned in her any defect; and she recommended to us to do the possible to avoid any slightest venial fault.

«As to mortal sin, — she said, signing her forehead, — my God, I believe that in the Houses of the Daughters of St. Anne it will never happen».

In her conferences she sometimes explained to us how venial sin can be committed, and that it must be avoided, because it too is a great offense to the Lord.

She was greatly grieved when she came to know that in one of our Houses gossip was not avoided, and to that Sister who had gossiped she said: «Take care, my daughter, before making Communion, try to go to confession». And she wished her also to ask pardon of the one about whom she had gossiped. Sometimes it happened that some Sister gossiped without realizing that it was gossip: then the Servant of God called her to herself, instructed her and made her understand how she had gossiped, and put her on her guard.

When the Servant of God spoke of the Passion, I saw tears fall from her eyes; and when in conferences, or speaking privately, her talk turned to the love of God, her face became a flame.

§ 613
Already as a child at the service of others.

Great was the charity of the Servant of God toward her neighbor, as the purpose of her Institute shows. Even when she was a lay person, she took as much as she could from the cares of the family to give herself to others, and then left her family to found her Institute.

Whether in instructing the ignorant or in assisting the sick, she always preferred the poor, and wished that her Institute too should have a preference for the poor.

Until the general cares of the Institute absorbed her entirely, she herself went through the Parishes to instruct the children, and this she did also as a lay person. I heard of various conversions wrought by her, but I cannot say either who or how. She admonished sinners, and first of all her brothers, as I heard her several times with regard to these.

She prayed for the conversion of sinners, and wanted us to pray, every time we went to church. When she was informed of some conversion wrought by her Sisters, great was the feast she made: «Come, listen», she said to us, and read us with great satisfaction the letter of information; and then she urged her Sisters to strive ever more to bring souls to God.

§ 614
Other founders also sought her counsel.

Proc. fol. 2288v.: Prudence: The Servant of God knew how to give timely counsel, and gave it as much to her daughters as to those who came to her, and these were not few, because all who found themselves in her presence felt seized with veneration and trust. Among the persons who had recourse to her for counsel, I know there were Founders and Foundresses of religious Institutes. I remember a certain Sister Savina, Foundress of the Sisters of Charity of St. Catherine of Siena, who came frequently to the Mother.

p. 396

From Mothers Carrega and Speranza I heard of a certain Fr. Francia, Founder of the Sisters of Zeal, called those of the poor man's morsel, in Palermo, who came to take counsel with our Mother.

From Mother Speranza I also heard it told that three so-called Nuns at Home, Sicilians, presented themselves to the Mother to seek counsel, feeling inspired to found Institutes, and that two of them really founded two different Institutes, which are doing well.

Persons of high station also came to her for counsel. I remember the Princess Odescalchi, of Piombino, of Fitalia and Alitieri, who often sought our Mother for counsel.

When she went on visitation to some House, the people of the City or town where she arrived flocked to her for counsel. To comfort her daughters who desired a word from her, a comfort from her, she spared no expense to have them come to her. And how well she knew how to console! A word from her was enough to put peace into even a most agitated heart.

§ 615
Prudence in counsel on vocation.

When she knew of some Sister who wavered a little in her vocation, she wrote to her in her own hand to encourage her, that she might reveal her inner self, and if she did not succeed, she had her come to her. If after speaking with these tempted ones for some hours she saw that she did not succeed, «well then, let us go to the Church, — she said, — to pray: you will give me the answer afterward». And after praying in the Church, peace had returned to the soul of that Sister, and she was already won. And this I saw many times. After the said prayer I heard the Mother say many times: «It is Jesus who has won her; it is Jesus who has consoled her». And to the Sister won she said: «It is Jesus who has won you», while the latter said: «I owe it to your prayers, O Mother, for before I felt so different».

I saw many letters addressed to the Mother, by reason of my office, with these expressions: «To you I owe it that I am still in the Institute»; and then thanks for her words, for her prayers, etc.

She seemed born on purpose to console her daughters in family misfortunes. In those days she took special care, keeping them near her, and did not abandon them.

§ 616
Just to all, grateful to benefactors.

Proc. fol. 2339v.: Justice: The Servant of God, far from being unjust to workmen, did not even know how to bargain in contracts with them, and gave what they asked. I heard her, however, sometimes say, after certain works were finished, when she noticed that the sum to be paid was exaggerated: «They eat me alive, these workmen. Perhaps because we are Sisters they take a little advantage». And to the agent of the works she recommended obtaining some reduction. When she charged her Sisters with certain expenses, she recommended them to ask for a discount.

Most grateful the Servant of God showed herself to those who did her Institute some favor, and if they were people to whom, because of their position, it was not fitting to give compensation in money, she made them some gift in objects. And she taught the Superiors to do the same.

§ 617
Most temperate and much mortified.

The Servant of God was most temperate in everything. Of a very sensitive character, she moderated her expressions. I never saw her angry, even in the gravest cases. In these I did see her weep sometimes, but not become angry, nor utter a word of complaint against the cause of her sorrow: at most she said to us: «This thing truly should not have happened: but God permits it; His will be done». After this she withdrew to the Church or to her room; and if we pressed to stay around her to comfort her, she said: «No, daughters, leave me alone». After a little we saw her tranquil, as if nothing had happened.

As to food, hers was a perfect fast.

When I came definitively to be with the Mother, in 1894, she still continued in her regimen of food, of strict meatless fast, seasoning of oil, and without use of wine. Then some time later, we speaking of it to the Cardinal Protector, that he might oblige her to moderate such rigor, she was obliged by him to use butter. We made these representations to the Cardinal Protector because the doctor warned us of our Mother's needs. Similarly, obliged by the Cardinal Protector, she had to use a little wine; and in this the Servant of God had to suffer not a little, being wholly unaccustomed; and so too, by the same obedience, she began to take an egg now and then.

When the Servant of God received these obediences from the Cardinal Protector, she turned to us and said: «You have played me a trick». As to the use of milk, I recall nothing.

p. 398

Apart from these exceptions made through obedience in the last years, her habitual food, even as a Religious, was this: broth made with herbs, boiled potatoes, fish, salads and legumes.

As to fish, Mother Carrega sometimes tried to have it very good for her, and sometimes went out to buy it herself, and I then heard the Mother say to Carrega: «Who knows how much you paid for this fish! But do not do these things for me again». When she was at Piacenza, Mother Carrega sometimes procured sturgeon for her, which is easy to get, because it is fished in the Po, when passing through, and the Servant of God said it was too delicious for her.

Poverty: The Servant of God was always patched, and patched herself, in the evening, when she went to her room, although we offered, begging her to let us do it. Sometimes, however, Mother Carrega secretly took away her old habit, substituting a new one; but the Servant of God, though forced to put on the new, because the old had been taken away, said: «I am never so well as with my old things» and asked it back of Carrega, who was forced to give it back.

She had, however, one unpatched habit, which she tried to keep nice for when she went to the Pope, and she called it: the Pope's habit.

When she died, however, we did not find even the Pope's habit decent enough to dress her in, and we had to be content with that one, because there was nothing better. Her petticoats too were of ordinary stuff, and she did not want even these replaced by new ones when they were old. The same is to be said of chemises, stockings, undershirts, etc.; and she had, in a word, everything old and patched. She was, however, most clean, and recommended cleanliness to us too. Habitually she wore cloth shoes, but sometimes I saw her in leather shoes. She used laundry soap to wash. If she noticed that some Sister had used perfumed soap, she reproved her.

Most poor was her room here in Rome: I do not speak of her secret room at Piacenza, already described. Of this, however, I shall say that in the last years one could no longer drag oneself up there except with great difficulty because of the narrowness of the little stair. Yet sometimes one dragged oneself up all the same. We then begged her to choose as her bedroom the one in which she worked and received the Sisters. In this there were some ordinary chairs, no armchair, a desk, a kneeler of common wood, a bed with a simple straw pallet without a mattress. The mattress she did not want even in the last days of her life. She had two pillows, just as in her room at Rome. There was a chest of drawers, a screen, a picture of Our Lady with the Child, a St. Anne and a Crucifix. But in that room she slept little.

The furnishing of her room at Rome was this. Besides the bed, as we said, there was an ordinary little table, covered with black oilcloth, with the Crucifix on it, which is now in the Chapel; another little table like the other, with a drawer, in which she kept her things. She had no bedside table. There were ordinary chairs, a rush-seated kneeler.

§ 619
In many ways she manifested her fortitude as foundress and as superior.

Proc. fol. 2496: Fortitude: The Servant of God, especially in the foundation and also in the governance of her Institute, naturally had many difficulties to overcome, but, from what I have heard said and from what I know directly, she never gave herself up as beaten, nor was ever disheartened, but went on constant and firm in her work.

Many of the things I have already said show her fortitude, such as the abandonment of her natural family to found the Institute; as when the son-in-law brought her the whole family at Piacenza, planting it on her there.

In 1891, on the occasion of the last illness of her son Alessandro at Piacenza, the Servant of God was here in Rome. Learning of his worsening, she did send two Sisters to assist and prepare him, but she did not move, nor was about to move. The Bishop of Piacenza, Mgr. Scalabrini, who visited Alessandro from time to time, seeing that he desired to see his mother again, telegraphed or wrote to her himself, saying: «Leave the affairs of the Institute for the moment, and come to do your duty», as the Servant of God herself afterward told me. She obeyed, and assisted him to death. When Alessandro entered his agony, she sent her Sisters home, and kneeling beside her son's bed for seven continuous hours she stayed there praying, without shedding a tear. Mgr. Scalabrini, who told me these details, said to me: «I have never seen so strong a woman».

p. 400

§ 620
She did not yield to weariness in the fulfillment of her office.

Proc. fol. 2505v.: She never yielded either to weariness or to her fragile health in the duties of her office. Even in the last days of her life, although her handwriting had become almost illegible, and although because of heart attacks she was often overtaken by sleep, she resisted, and wished to content her distant daughters at least with a few lines in her own hand.

I recall that in the letters she wrote me, among other things she said to me: «Do not be disheartened, be strong, whatever happens to you, the Holy Mother is at your side». And I know she made similar exhortations to the other Superiors as well.

§ 621
Extraordinarily delicate in chastity.

As to chastity, I shall say first of all that the Servant of God did not permit herself to be touched by anyone, not even by the Doctor, whom only in the last times she allowed to feel her pulse. How many times I offered to put her shoes on for her, her feet being so swollen, and she did not permit it. In the last years, however, no longer able to bend, she was then obliged to have this service done by the infirmarian. After I had been in the Hospitals, however, she let me take her pulse. She never let herself be seen undressed by us, and when we saw her suffering, we begged her to call us at least when she had gone to bed, and she did so.

I never heard her speak of her marriage, and I never heard her speak of her husband, nor even pronounce his name.

§ 622
Always accompanied when speaking with lay people.

With lay people she always presented herself accompanied, and if anyone had come asking to speak alone with the Mother: «Oh, that is impossible», she answered. And this caution of the rule of always being two together, how she recommended it to us too! If she came to know that some Superior permitted herself to appear alone with lay people, one may say she saw no more and gave herself no peace. She tried to ascertain, and as long as she could she herself went in person to ascertain and to put the Superior in her place.

I remember a certain Superior who, in her justification, in sometimes receiving lay people alone alleged the too small number of Sisters she had with her, so that while the others attended to urgent duties she by necessity had to receive alone lay people whom, owing to circumstances, she could not have sent away. «Well then, — the Servant of God answered her, — if these reasons are the true ones, I sacrifice myself to send you one more Sister», and so she did. And this caution not only with lay seculars she used and wished to be used also by the Sisters, but also with Priests.

I remember that in the conferences to the Novitiate, explaining how the vow of chastity must be guarded, among other things she told us not to gesticulate so much, not to touch one another, and she did not permit this even in jest, nor that we take one another by the arm even for a moment, nor give the hand. She herself gave the example by her very dignified bearing and without gesticulations.

§ 623
Perfect obedience to authorities.

Proc. fol. 2522v.: The Servant of God was most obedient to all her Superiors, beginning with the Pope, the Sacred Congregation, the Protector. As to the Confessor, we infer that she was most obedient to him too, because if sometimes we told him that out of charity he should make the Servant of God take this or that thing, we saw afterward that she took it, whereas before she resisted our insistence. She herself called us, her Assistants, to counsel, and we could freely express our opinions, which she took into account. She first let us speak, and then stated her opinion, asking us what we said of it, and so it happened that sometimes we yielded, sometimes she yielded.

She recommended obedience to us much, and said to the Superiors that if they wished to obtain obedience from their subjects, they had to give the example of this virtue themselves first. She was wont to say, as I heard her more than once, that she found no greater happiness than being faithful to her rule and to the common schedule.

§ 624
Most loving of humility.

As to humility, the Servant of God never welcomed praise, and if she heard any, she at once signed her forehead, as I saw many times. Woe if she had heard praises of herself from us! Without fail she scolded us and said to us: «If you see anything good in us, it is not I, but God who has done it. I am only a little mustard seed cast into arid ground».

If she heard some Sister say: «I did this, I did that», she interrupted saying: «Oh, this blessed I!». And once I heard her say to a Sister: «You should rather say, I, my donkey!». I never heard that she in any way praised or exalted her own works or those of the Institute. I heard her say many times: «I am a poor wretch: I am the donkey; and if God did not assist me, poor work of His!». And these words she said when she saw the Institute exalted and praised. She also said that she did not like the Institute to be exalted, because then she trembled. «I desire rather that the Institute be opposed and afflicted, because then I am ever more confirmed that the work is of God». One saw that when she was despised, rather than being disturbed, she rejoiced in it, and said: «I deserve this and more».

§ 625
Photographed for reason of obedience.

She had herself photographed only ever through obedience. On the occasion of the first departure of our Sisters for America, they ill resigning themselves to going so far without her photograph, she was then for the first time ordered through obedience to have herself photographed. Of this obedience I heard speak not only from Sisters, but also from herself, who said: «Oh, that time they ordered me to pose!». This grieved her greatly, especially because it seemed to her she had given bad example to her Sisters. The second photograph was imposed on her by Cardinal Verga, at the urging of the Sisters; and it was taken in two poses, one seated and the other standing. And as the Servant of God adapted herself poorly, the Cardinal himself resigned himself to pose too, for the first time, to induce the Servant of God more easily. I know that the Cardinal's relatives showed themselves grateful to the Servant of God for having thus obtained the photograph of the Cardinal, who had never had himself photographed.

In the Theological virtues, in the Cardinal ones, in the exercise of the vows, and in the other virtues of which I have spoken, the Servant of God not only persevered to the end, but kept ever growing, as we Sisters could notice until the last day.

§ 626
She practiced the virtues in a manner superior to the common.

Ad 28: All the aforesaid virtues, none excluded, were practiced by the Servant of God not only in a manner far superior to the common run of pious souls, but with a constancy, with a facility, as if she possessed a second nature, as if they were connatural to her, as if she felt the need to act so and not otherwise, in a heroic degree and such as to surpass even the virtues practiced by many Saints who are venerated on the altars. And this is not my opinion only, but we speak of it always with this persuasion among us Sisters, and we say: «There will never have been another Foundress like ours!». We admire her, but truly we do not know how to imitate her.

p. 403

§ 627
Prophetic spirit.

Ad 30: When Monsignor Granito di Belmonte had not yet come to Rome to begin his diplomatic career, as Mother Benedetta Carrega told me, the Servant of God said of him: «He will be Cardinal, and Protector of our Institute».

When the Servant of God was for the last time in Messina, having seen the girls of our boarding school, afterward, speaking with us (I was there too, accompanying her), to the question of the local Superior as to what she had thought of her pupils, I recall that of Miss Maria Patti she said: «That one will one day be our Sister and an edifying Sister», and this Miss is today our exemplary Religious, Sr. Anna Vittoria. And yet at that time, both because of her age of 14 or 15 and because of her natural liveliness, she had given no sign of vocation. Indeed not even immediately afterward did she give any such sign: she was intent on her studies, which she loved, and that was all.

I have heard it said that of various Sisters she foresaw the recovery, while death was expected. For example: sometimes the blessing for a sister in danger of life was asked by telegram from the house, and she answered: «The blessing yes, I send it, but the Sister will not die». And the Sister did not die.

Ad 32, Proc. fol. 2534: I read, before it was withdrawn, the book of the Servant of God «Labors and Consolations», as I have already deposed. The Servant of God also wrote some short prayers, and I know of nothing else. I have heard it said, however, that she wrote something on penances.

In no writing of the Servant of God, including the letters, did I ever find anything that does not befit a holy soul.

§ 628
Serenity and fortitude in the last illnesses.

Ad 33: Before the last journey the Servant of God made, she was already in very poor health. She wished nevertheless to make it, to go to Ovada Ligure. Our Doctor Montechiari, however, advised us not to make our Mother travel all in one stretch, but to break the journey, having her rest one night at Pisa; and so it was done. Of the four Sisters who accompanied her, however, Carrega and Speranza stayed with her, while I and Sr. A. Borromea went on to Ovada. That night at Pisa the Servant of God felt ill. The Sisters wished to call the doctor, who was not a little astonished that we should make a woman in such a state of health travel, since, he said, she has a heart attack, and should neither travel nor tire herself.
