Having recovered a little, however, the Servant of God resumed the journey to Ovada the next day, and we reached our House of the Castle of Lercara. This journey, I do not remember well whether it was made in the month of May or June of 1899, or after the feast of St. Anne. I remember, however, this detail: that it was about that month, in which we stayed at Lercara, that we received the news of the death of Cardinal Verga, our Protector. There, although she did not recover completely, as she perhaps hoped, she visited that House, heard the Sisters, and going up and down, two other Houses near Ovada, of which she also made the visitation. Afterward we went to Sestri Ponente for the visitation of our House, and here too we stayed a good little while. Then finally we were at our House of Sampierdarena, where we also carried out the visitation. In the days of our stay in this House, Sr. A. Brigida, one of the first Sisters of the Institute, was seized by a heart attack, and the Servant of God, before she died (which happened the very night of the attack), wished, despite the near impossibility, to climb the stairs to go and see her, and bring her her blessing, which the dying woman had keenly desired. She heard all the Sisters (Sr. A. Brigida had been heard before she died), visited the House, reviewed the accounts, and then we went to our House of Genoa. How much trouble it was to get the Mother up from the little square below our House, where the carriage could not go up. That climb had to be made bit by bit, and with the help of a chair. On the day of our arrival we advised her to go to bed early, because she was worn out, and she heeded us. She carried out slowly the visitation of this House too. After some days, one morning before the wake-up bell, I hear myself called by Sr. A. Serafina Foglia: «Quick, quick, for the Mother feels ill». I go into her room and she says to me: «I feel ill, you know. I tried to get up, and I cannot». I take her pulse and I saw things were bad, because the pulse was fluttering and sometimes vanished. I ran to Sr. A. Celsa Speranza to tell her that the Mother was ill, very ill. They got out of bed at once, Carrega and Speranza, and hurried over, and among us it was agreed to call a good doctor, without saying anything to the Mother. The doctor came at once, but in the meantime the Servant of God showed a desire to receive Communion, and, the Chaplain having arrived for Mass, she was satisfied. The doctor, having arrived afterward, taking her pulse, said: «The case is grave: if we save her it is a miracle: her heart is very weak». But the Servant of God did not want to be auscultated or examined. The doctor warned us not to abandon her even a minute; he ordered her a medicine to raise the heart, prescribed complete rest, and that she should not get out of bed.

Proc. fol. 2540: The Servant of God having improved a little, the doctor permitted her after a number of days to get out of bed. She slowly carries out the visitation of her House, which had many Sisters. The return journey to Rome giving us concern, where the Servant of God absolutely wished to come before winter began, we begged the doctor to be willing to accompany us. Fr. Agostino Donadio happened to be in Genoa in the days of the return, and since he had to return to Rome, we begged him to come with us. We traveled by night, and there was no harm. She suffered, yes, but we feared worse. Here the doctor ordered her absolute rest, saying to her: «You must not work mentally, and must not occupy yourself with anything»; and in this state she was handed over to Doctor Montechiari, who said to us: «Do not deceive yourselves; we shall have the Mother only a little while: it is finished».

§ 629
She never abandoned herself to complete rest.

The Servant of God, however, never abandoned herself to complete rest. By dint of our prayers we managed to obtain that she rise a little later in the morning. Having improved a little, she always worked; she dispatched the mail; in the morning she wrote.

In those days came the occasion of the Episcopal Consecration of Monsignor Granito di Belmonte Pignatelli, and the Servant of God dealt directly with the upholsterer to adorn our Church. Only in the last days did she allow herself to lean on the arm of some Sister to support herself walking about the house. We always said at home that the Servant of God suffered from heart attacks, and that a progressive paralysis had begun in her. Her heart, however, no one had yet listened to. Toward the end of 1899, or at the beginning of 1900, Sr. A. Maria Teresa Sorrentino comes for a few days and takes part in our solicitude for the Mother. One day she says to me: «But how is it that everyone says the Mother has heart attacks, whereas she tells me that she has not had a heart for a long time?». I, then, speaking with the doctor, who told me the Mother's heart was going very badly, urged him to listen to it. «But how to do it? — he answers me, — she does not permit it». And I: «Let us do this. Place yourself at the Mother's left, while she is seated, and so speaking, by surprise, put your ear to her chest and listen». He did so, and the aim was achieved. The Mother, surprised, let it be done, but then said to me: «They want to find my heart: but I have not had a heart for a long time!». And after a moment, repenting of having let such expressions escape, she added: «Oh, pay no attention to my words!».

The Servant of God continued to work, less badly, until the beginning of April. In the last three months of life, however, she no longer slept as one should sleep, but was in a continual drowsiness by day and by night and could no longer rest her head on the pillows. If she rested it a little, her breath failed her, and the doctor recommended to us never to leave her alone. Mother Carrega and Mother Speranza, when the Servant of God withdrew to her room, assisted her until midnight, from midnight onward I and Sr. A. Serafina Foglia. From time to time, however, the Servant of God said to us: «But what are you doing here? go to bed». I managed sometimes to make her sleep a few minutes, and once an hour, taking advantage of the moment when, seeing her head fall, I slowly brought the palm of my hand to her forehead, supporting it for her. That night when she slept an hour, she herself noticed it, looking at the clock, and feeling much relieved by that brief rest I had procured for her, oh how much gratitude she showed me: she never ceased thanking me, and in the morning she told it to all who presented themselves. Slowly the Servant of God grew worse until the first days of May. From the whole Institute they sent us telegrams and letters asking for news of the Mother, and also from many lay people; and we answered that they should pray, because she was slowly growing worse and we feared losing her. And triduums and novenas followed one another in our Houses for the Mother's recovery.

Her son-in-law, however, to Sr. A. Rosella Bolognini, then portress of this House, who told him that the Mother was ill and that, continuing so, we would have her only a little while, answered: «It is her head that is sick».

p. 407

§ 630
Will.

On returning from Genoa the Servant of God said to us at once in the first days: «Have the Notary Tommaso Monti called for me, for I wish to put my affairs in order». To our remarks as to what she could be thinking, and that she should think rather of recovering, she replied: «Oh, what is this, after all? It is a thing I should have done before too». The Notary having come, she remained alone with him, made her will and handed it to him. Soon afterward her brother Francesco arrived, to whom she spoke of the will then made. And he: «Yes, you did well, but now you must think rather of recovering».

§ 631
Chain of penance to the last moment.

In the first days of May triduums were held to Maria Mater Gratiae, to whom she had such devotion. The last three nights Jesus was kept always exposed in our Chapel. And the Novices followed one another continually for adoration. The last triduum to Our Lady finished, on the last Thursday before her death, whereas in the preceding days she scarcely ate anything any more, that morning she ate a little more and said to us: «I taste it too». All of us happy said to one another: «Our Lady has worked the grace», we repeated it through the whole house. Instead it was the day of her collapse. The meal finished we went up at once to her, rejoicing, and she took part in our gladness. The moment of the spiritual reading having come, she said to us: «You go to the reading, while I retire to my room». All of us of the Secretariat accompanied her to her room, and walking she leaned on our arms because she staggered. I no longer deceived myself at all, from the practice I had of hospitals, and so too thought Sr. A. Amante La Barbera. Mother Carrega, however, and Mother Speranza hoped to the end. We had sat down for the reading when Sr. A. Serafina, left in company with the Mother, comes out of the room asking urgently for pincers. «Quick, pincers, pincers». While we were thinking of going to the shoemaker Sister, Sr. A. Benedetta, who by chance had a pair bought for forty-eight, hands her her own. We stopped outside the door of the Servant of God, eager to enter, but the Servant of God said to us: «One moment, one moment, and then you will enter; leave me meanwhile alone with Sr. A. Serafina». What had happened in that time? When we left her to go to the reading, she began to feel very ill and to swell extremely. A tumor she had in her body, as we saw afterward from the discharges she vomited, had burst, and a chain she wore all around her hips had sunk still deeper into the flesh; and then at last the Servant of God, who would never have wished to be seen or touched by a living soul, was obliged to make use of Sr. A. Serafina to have that chain unfastened from her hips. Sr. A. Serafina, as she afterward told us, could not unfasten it, so deeply had it become embedded in the flesh. As soon as she had broken it with the pincers, however, the Servant of God took it off herself with great ease. Sr. A. Serafina was under the obligation of silence, and in those last days said nothing, keeping that chain secretly. After the death, however, she handed it to Mother Benedetta, and we were able to see it: it was bloodstained.

We having entered after that brief moment of waiting, in which Sr. Serafina broke her chain, we obliged her to lie down, and helped her undress. And while we helped her undress, she continued in her vomiting. Lying down, I cut her bodice with scissors, because she could not help herself and we could not manage to take it off. I was obliged also to cut part of her chemise over the chest and to cover her as best I could, because she had been soiled with the pus that came with the vomit. We were all weeping. I do not remember well whether it was that same day or that night that she desired to have in her room the dear little image of Mary, Mater Gratiae et Misericordiae, of the Venerable Clausi, of which a facsimile is kept in our Chapel, because the original was requested of us by the General of the Minims after the death of Fr. Agostino Donadio, Postulator of the Order. It was placed before her on the little table, and she remained absorbed in prayer. I know, but I was not present, that later she wished to rise a little to go and adore her little Madonna close at hand, but she could not kneel.

§ 633
Absorbed in prayer in the last days.

In those last two days the Servant of God was always absorbed in prayer, and it could be seen from the glance she turned from time to time to her Crucifix.

The Mother noticed once that Sisters Carrega and Speranza had been absent for a little while. She suspected, as was in fact the case, that they were weeping in some corner, and said to me: «Where are Sr. Benedetta and Sr. Celsa? They will be weeping. But do not weep. What more can I do down here for you? Better I shall help you from Paradise».

p. 409

Proc. fol. 2549: The last words of the Servant of God which I reported in the last session were on the Friday before her death. We never abandoned her; and she always wanted us around her, as could be seen from her glance round about, which sought us. The Barbiellini relatives were seen in those days more rarely, because they did not believe in the gravity of the illness, although we had told them.

On Friday morning, as also on Saturday morning, the Servant of God made her Communion.

§ 634
Her last words before dying.

For dinner naturally we took turns, and that Friday Sr. A. Celsa Speranza and Sr. A. Serafina Foglia went down first to dinner, and these having returned, Sr. A. Amante and I went down. But behold, after brief moments the Servant of God had us called. We ran at once, but she, seized by a fit, being no longer able to repeat to us well what she had said before to Sr. A. Celsa, told it to us indeed, as best she could, but Sr. Celsa herself repeated it to us, because we could not understand her well, and these were the words, looking at her Crucifix: «I have finished suffering: all is averted, the Institute, I hope, will triumph». At these words we understood everything and could not hold back our tears. She looked at us sadly, and wholly absorbed in God. And for a time she did not even try to speak. She crossed her fingers and so remained until the last breath.

One night when she was being watched, for a moment only Sr. Serafina and I remained with the Servant of God, who questioned her thus: «Would the Mother not wish to live still?». And she in intelligible accents answered: «To do the will of God and for his work I would gladly live even to a hundred years; but this I assure you, that the day of my death will be the most beautiful of my life».

§ 635
Serene death.

On Sunday morning about half past nine the Servant of God rendered her soul to her Lord. At that moment all of us of the Secretariat, together with Sr. A. Consolata Massinelli, who had arrived the evening before, and Sr. A. Amante La Barbera, were present. Also present were Fr. Agostino Donadio, Fr. Vincenzo d'Alatri and Don Emanuelli, then Chaplain of our House, and now Bishop in Sardinia. Also there were the two brothers of the Servant of God and the Barbiellini.

The last services to the Servant of God were rendered by Sr. A. Serafina Foglia, Sr. A. Rosella Bolognini and Sr. A. Consolata Massinelli.

§ 636
Signs of penance on the body.

Ad 34: From Sr. A. Serafina Foglia I learned at once that various signs had been found on the body of the Servant of God: a deep wound on the side of the heart, and here and there scars of little chains and hair shirts.

The Provincial of Sicily, Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi, hurried over with other Superior Sisters to see the Mother again, but found her dead; and having heard of this deep wound on the side of the heart found on the body of the Servant of God, she wished to see it; but it was too late, for, however much she tried, the body having swollen extraordinarily, it was not possible for her.

§ 637
Intervention of the Visitor at the death of the Servant of God.
§ 638
Inventory of the room and attitude of the son-in-law.

The Servant of God being dead, I was not present at the services rendered to her, because I had to deal with the Notary and with the Barbiellini. The night before, that is between Saturday and Sunday, Sr. A. Michelina Negri had heard the granddaughter Maria say to her father that he should take care to put the seals on as soon as the grandmother died. But the evening before there had arrived here unexpectedly the Apostolic Visitor Monsignor Serafini, although he himself had not thought of nor knew of the gravity of the Servant of God's illness; for it too had escaped us to think of notifying him. But the Lord made use of Barbiellini himself, who sent him a telegram at Subiaco, where he then was, worded more or less thus: «The Mother is gravely ill: come. B.». From this initial B he thought that Sr. A. Benedetta had sent it to him, and he hurried at once. Seeing the gravity of the case, and having given his blessing to the sick woman, who no longer understood, he turned to us to give us timely counsel for the moment. «Mind, — he said to us, — that the relatives may play some trick; and if there is a will, as I know there is, it will be well for the Notary to come at once: indeed I myself, now returning to the Monastery, will pass by the Notary to warn him to be here tomorrow morning. It will be opportune to proceed at once to an inventory of the room of the Servant of God, the body being present». In fact, the next morning, even before the Servant of God expired, the Notary Tommaso Monti was with us; and when, the death having occurred, Count Gaspare Barbiellini was getting ready to carry out his plans, the Notary, Fr. Agius, Secretary of the Apostolic Visitor (absent because that morning he was being consecrated Bishop), Sr. A. Santina Solenghi, and I being present, said: «Gently, Mr. Count, there is a will to be respected». Count Gaspare Barbiellini then flared up, saying that we had taken advantage of that poor woman, and said various insolent things to Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega, who, called at that moment, had come: but she did not answer, and said: «I do not answer: let Fr. Agius answer for me». The inventory was proceeded with at once, Sr. A. Solenghi, I, Count Barbiellini, the daughter Maria, the Lawyer called by us, and two witnesses being present. That is, the daughter Maria was still to be present, but this happened: that, we having entered the room of the Servant of God to proceed to the inventory, Maria opened the wall cupboard, where the Servant of God was wont to put her few things, and finding it almost empty, as usual, turned to her father, saying: «They have spirited everything away». And then, turning to her grandmother, laid on her bed, she said: «As grandmother I respect you, but as General I make war on you». And she ran off without wishing to return again, although her father insisted.

The remains of the Servant of God stayed exposed in her room all Sunday and Monday. Many people came to see her, besides our Sisters, notified by telegram; many Sisters of other Institutes also came, and also many lay people of every class, and Priests.

§ 639
Reputation for holiness and funeral.

The word on everyone's lips was that a Saint had died. Mgr. Vincenzo Sardi, who had not known her in life and who for the first time saw the body on the deathbed, came out of her room in ecstasy and gave a most beautiful funeral eulogy for her on the thirtieth day.

A Priest, whom I did not know, coming out of the room of the Servant of God said to me: «I realized that I had prayed before a Saint». I do not know what came from that face to make such an impression.

Proc. fol. 2557v: Our Sisters touched the body of the Servant of God with rosaries and other objects of piety: I could not say particulars.

On Monday evening, 7 May 1900, the body was placed in a triple coffin, one of which was of zinc; and with the body was enclosed a tube containing a parchment, bearing the principal dates of the Servant of God, and signed by the Vicar Mother. I know that Barbiellini wished his own name to be added as well, and those of his family. The same evening she was carried to the Chapel on the first floor. I must note here that the third coffin was added the following day, Tuesday, when she was carried into the Church for the funeral. A great many people attended, so that the Church was filled. Most of our Sisters were in the choir loft.

§ 640
Burial of the Servant of God.

Ad 35: The funeral over, that same Tuesday morning, she was transported to the Cemetery. All our Sisters attended, and there were very many. The brothers of the Mother also attended, and many outsiders, but not the Barbiellini, who showed themselves only at the moment when the hearse was ready to move toward the Cemetery. I do not remember well whether, with the Count, the daughter Maria or the son Camillo gave a smile, and then withdrew. Carlotta did not show herself. Many poor people benefited by her were still present, who had tears in their eyes, saying: «We have lost our Benefactress».

In the Cemetery she was laid in a tomb of the quadrangle; here she stayed a year, until the Chapel was built on the Pincetto, at the Institute's expense (and Mr. Francesco Gattorno took charge of the direction). And here she was laid definitively the following year above the entrance door of the Chapel itself. Here the outer walnut coffin no longer exists, because it has all rotted.

§ 641
Frequent visits to the tomb.

Ad 37: I, especially in the first years after the death of the Servant of God, went very often with other Sisters to the tomb of our Mother; and in those first years our Novices, by turns, went there every day. Other Sisters wrote to Mother Carrega that they had received graces through the intercession of the Servant of God, and asked permission to come to Rome to venerate her tomb, having made a vow, if they should receive the grace.

The tomb of our venerated Mother was our comfort. At our Chapel in the Cemetery we have many times seen other persons unknown to us who were praying.

In these last times, however, we having greatly thinned out our visits, it has not happened to me to find other persons there praying. Yet there is no grace we desire, no comfort we ask, without our going to the tomb of our Mother, and finding ourselves heard. There is no Sister who arrives in Rome who does not, as her first thing, ask to go to the tomb of our Mother.

p. 413

This concourse has always been spontaneous, as appears from what has already been said.

The Princess of Fitalia, when she comes to Rome, never fails to go to the Mother's tomb and to have Mass celebrated at the altar of the Chapel; indeed I shall say that this Lady, every time she comes to Rome, spends hours in prayer in the room where the Servant of God died; and when the Prince her consort comes to fetch her, she, before taking leave of us, induces him too to pray in the said room. Her sister, Madame Trepka, a Pole, having come once to Rome, wished to go and visit our Mother in the Cemetery. I myself accompanied her there, and she said to me: «I came to Italy also for my sister, but still more to visit the tomb of the Servant of God, whom I knew in life and from whom I received graces».

§ 642
Growing reputation for holiness. Requests for relics.

Ad 38: As to the reputation for holiness of the Servant of God, during her life it was among us Sisters that she was a Saint worthy of the Altars, that she was a worker of graces and miracles. When the Sisters came to this House, certainly not of the Servant of God did they ask for things she had used, but they did ask us of the Secretariat, to make use of them afterward with devotion either in cases of illness or for other spiritual needs of theirs.

When I left for the second time for America, seeing that the Servant of God had prepared two or three pairs of stockings for the Sisters, I asked her to favor me with them. And she: «What do you want to do with them?». And having answered her that I would give a pair to some of those Superiors in America, she agreed, and not only that, but then knitted other pairs, as many as there were Superiors there. Arrived in America, I distributed to the Superiors those various pairs of stockings, and they, oh! how they appreciated the gift, both because it was the work of their Mother, and for the kind thought she had had. They then kept them as relics, and from time to time I saw letters arriving from these Superiors, who told me: «I lent that pair of stockings to one or another Sister ill in the legs, and she was cured». They then in fact used them for any ailment.

At table not only the Novices but also the Professed shared the crumbs and little bits of bread left over by the Servant of God, and this out of devotion.

p. 414

Not only our Sisters esteemed her a Saint, but all those who saw her and conversed with her.

I remember that a minister plenipotentiary of Bolivia to the French Republic, a certain Don Luis Paz, came to Rome with his whole family and wished to see the Servant of God also. After he had conversed with her, I remember that in the corridor, as he was leaving, he said to us: «But what a great woman you have for Mother: you have a Saint». He too wished to be called a son of our Mother or of St. Anne.

A certain Mr. Cacace of Taranto, who died this year, founded an orphanage, where he called our Sisters, and decreed that the care should never be entrusted to anyone but our Sisters; but this did not happen definitively until after he had seen and dealt with the Servant of God, who produced in him, an atheist, a very strong impression. We still keep a letter of his written at that time, and another afterward in which he speaks of his conversation with our Mother, and there are these expressions, more or less: «Those eyes of heaven, that face of a Saint, etc.».

I remember a certain Mr. La Monica, I think of Castiglione di Sicilia, who had a quite special devotion to the Servant of God because of her reputation for holiness. He came to Rome once to see her, and in Sicily, as soon as he knew that the Servant of God was there, wherever she might be, he went at once to pay her a visit. I remember having seen several letters of his to the Servant of God, in which he professed deep veneration to her.

I know of many others, whom I cannot now specify, who held the Servant of God in esteem as a Saint, because they themselves said so.

After the death of the Servant of God this reputation for holiness not only was maintained among our Sisters and outsiders, but grew and grows ever more, so that we cannot rid ourselves of requests for relics and images of the Servant of God. The Superiors write to us continually on behalf of other outside persons. Many Ladies have asked us for images for their sons who are going to war.

After our Libyan war, as we were going from Livorno to Pisa, we met an Army Captain, who on seeing us drew from his wallet the image of our Mother, saying to us: «I was in the Libyan war, and I am safe because of this».

p. 415

Two or three years after the death of the Servant of God the present Bishop of Castellammare di Stabia, who was then Bishop of Bovino, came to this House, and spoke to us with very great enthusiasm of the holiness of our Mother; and had it depended on him, he would already have put her on the altars. I also remember that Cardinal Gennari, already when he was Bishop of Conversano, I, who was then Superior at Noci, going to him, he spoke to me of our Mother as of a Saint whom we must imitate; and after her death I remember that he, a Cardinal, still spoke to us of her as of a Saint, and said to us: «You have lost a Saint». All this reputation for holiness was certainly not promoted by any artifice, but is wholly spontaneous.

Ad quaest. ex off., Proc. fol. 2570: Questioned ex officio, the Witness declared that she does not know that the Servant of God used Teaching Diplomas to have those lacking them give school, substituting persons by deceit, but she does know, on the contrary, that the holder of the school who had the diploma, although supplied by another Sister who did not have it, was nevertheless always the one provided with the diploma who was responsible before the Superintendent.

§ 643
Clarifications on some points of the life of the Servant of God.

Additamentum eiusdem testis, Proc. fol. 2591v.: After the death of the Servant of God Barbiellini presented against us to the Congregation of the Council a document with the signature of the Servant of God, in which she professed herself a debtor to him of fifty thousand lire. In the Servant of God's own hand, however, there was only the signature, and it bore no date. This signature was wrested from the Servant of God in the following way. In 1899, while she was at Sestri Ponente for the visitation of her houses, her granddaughter Maria arrived there with her mother. Maria had with her a sheet of stamped paper and begged the Servant of God to be willing to affix her signature on that sheet, because, she said, we have learned in the surest manner that at such and such a Bank there are still some funds of poor Alessandro, and we cannot withdraw them without your signature. The Servant of God answered: «But no, there is nothing left». «Yes, yes, — Maria resumed, — we know for certain, there is still something. Put your signature, and if then there is nothing, it will be little harm; but we know that there is». And so the Servant of God was induced to affix her signature. Her brother Francesco then coming to see her, the Servant of God told him that Carlotta and Maria had been with her, and had told her that there was something of Alessandro's at the Bank, for the withdrawal of which her signature was necessary, and that she had satisfied them, signing a blank paper. Francesco disapproved of that signature, saying to her: «You did wrong». «But why?» the Servant of God resumed. And Francesco: «Because one must never sign anything in blank. One does not know what may come out». From that moment the Servant of God had no peace. And seeing her agitated, and asking her what was the matter, she told us what had happened. She then wrote to Maria, who was at Piacenza, asking for the return of her blank signature, because at the Bank there should no longer be anything of Alessandro's. And Maria answered her that in fact there was nothing left, and therefore that sheet bearing the blank signature had been burned. The Servant of God, however, did not rest, and insisted, until Maria and Carlotta, returning to her, Maria dared to swear on the Crucifix that she had really burned the said sheet.

The Servant of God was then perplexed, and for her own peace of mind made a counter-deed through a Notary. All the rest I learned from the Mother herself, except the counter-deed, which I learned after her death.

Asked, I declare that the grandchildren of the Servant of God, coming to our House, came by the stairs of the guesthouse and went to the grandmother's office, and therefore there was no disturbance for the Community nor noise that could disturb the Community.

Between Sr. Anna del Salvatore Orsi and our Mother there were relations of intimacy; but of these I know no particulars. I recall only this episode from when I was Superior at Borgo San Donnino.

Sr. A. del Salvatore had been slandered, I do not know of what. The Servant of God then summoned the Superiors to Piacenza for a course of Exercises. I could not attend because of the great deal I had to do. I was present, however, at the closing, as the Servant of God had wished. I remember that a Provincial proposed to all the Superiors to go to the Servant of God to ask pardon for Sr. A. del Salvatore; a proposal which was accepted by all.

Meanwhile Sr. Anna del Salvatore was quietly praying in the Church, where I went to see her, and I saw her in profile.

We entered, then, to the Servant of God to ask her pardon, as I said. To our words the Servant of God answered: «But pardon for what? Sr. A. del Salvatore has no fault at all, and I am ready to embrace her».

From that day the relations between the two were very close.

I do not know how long afterward, the Servant of God having returned to Palermo, I saw her again. Now it seems to me that, before this visit, I had seen her again another time at Piacenza and at Rome.

My interest in the Servant of God was gradually growing, and also my affection. Visit followed visit, at Palermo, in Rome, at Piacenza, until at last I entered into intimacy, and this happened especially after the death of Sr. A. del Salvatore.

Sr. A. del Salvatore spoke to me of the Servant of God as of a great Saint, and told me so many things that I no longer remember. The late Mother Carrega also spoke to me of her with the same enthusiasm, and so too the present Mother General Sr. A. Celsa Speranza, but I do not remember the particulars. Since the death of the Servant of God I have had much intimacy with Sr. A. Serafina Foglia, who has told me many, many things about the Servant of God, and of these I recall few.

§ 656
Great affection and admiration for the Servant of God.

Ad 8: The Servant of God was very fond of me, as can be seen from the letters she addressed to me two or three times a week, and which I for the most part have already handed over to the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne. The rest I am going through now, and once I have gone through them, I shall hand them over likewise as the others. I returned the Servant of God's affection with equal affection, and this grew so much that I loved her more than my own carnal mother, whom I also loved tenderly. By her I had myself directed in every smallest thing, both spiritual and temporal. In life she had promised me that when I invoked her I should always find her at my side. After her death I have invoked her and invoke her very frequently every day, and I find indeed verified what she promised me, and it seems to me that I feel her near me.

After God, the Most Holy Virgin and St. Joseph, my prayers are always directed to her. From this it is understood how I would so much wish her to be sanctified, and soon. I submit naturally to the judgment of the Holy See, which I hope, however, will be very favorable.

§ 657
Family life.

Ad 9: Of her childhood I remember little. I believe it was of this time that the fact I heard from her occurred: that, being at the villa, and the family having forbidden her to go to Church, early in the morning she climbed over the wall of the villa, although it was high.

p. 429

XXXI witness (IV ex off.), Mrs. E. Settimo Princ. of Fitalia 429

She was very fond of her parents, and then was fond of her husband, but of him she did not speak to me, except for some allusion, as for example to his death.

She told me that her family sometimes took her against her will to the theater, but she never saw anything, because she fell asleep. And I know nothing else.

Of her married life, as I have already said, she never spoke to me, and I had this impression: that she would have wished almost to erase this period from her life. She spoke to me, however, with great affection of her children. She said she had felt a deep love, and that when she lost the third of her children, she went to the feet of Our Lady of Sorrows, feeling as if she would almost go mad, and that then she felt comforted, and the rest I no longer remember.

§ 658
Her husband dead, she devoted herself to piety and charity.

Ad 16: In widowhood she occupied herself much with pious works, which were entrusted to her or almost imposed on her by the Archbishop of Genoa. She busied herself much with the sick, and in the Hospitals spent whole nights and days. She herself told me that sometimes she had herself shut in the Church to stay there in prayer. Once, having gone out early in the morning, and finding the door of the Church still closed, and being afraid of some youths who were following her, she pushed the door of the Church, which opened and shut again immediately behind her. At the hour of opening, the sacristan arriving, he was very surprised to see this woman praying before the Sacrament. This is her own account.

The Archbishop advised her to come to Rome to consult the Supreme Pontiff Pio Nono, and she left, accompanied by a friend.

She returned to Genoa by way of Piacenza, and on the journey toward Piacenza a Priest who was in the same compartment, in conversation, hearing that they were seeking a House for an Institute, invited her and her friend to stop for this purpose at Piacenza, where she would easily find a house. The Servant of God agreed; at Piacenza she bought the house, which was in a horrible state and therefore for little, and then returned to Genoa to arrange her affairs.

Proc. fol. 2702: The reason why she began her Institute not at Genoa but at Piacenza was, according to what she told me, the advice given her by some Ecclesiastics, that it was better to found the Institute outside her native city.

Ad 22: The Servant of God was always Superior General of her Institute; but certainly she never desired it. I recall that she never wanted the number one to be used for numbering the linen, such number belonging, according to her, only to St. Anne; and almost as if she were not Superior, but St. Anne, she tied the key of the House of Piacenza to a small statuette of St. Anne which is on the stairs, and I believe that she still keeps the key of the House tied there.

She herself told me that in the beginnings of the Institute, returning once to the House of Piacenza, she was received there with much coldness, as if she were not even Superior, since there was a Sister who aspired to that office and was supported by an Ecclesiastic: she spent the whole night in prayer on the altar step. The next day she was ordered to humble and tiring services in the kitchen and refectory: she had to carry large, very heavy trays with dishes.

She often expressed to me the desire and the hope that one day Jesus would grant her the grace of no longer being Mother General, but of having a little corner where to spend the rest of her days praying.

Her office as General I have the absolute conviction that she fulfilled with sublime perfection, since besides being a Saint she was also of a brilliant intelligence, which extended to all sorts of things.

She also had extraordinary helps from the Lord. She told me, as to the acceptance of Postulants, that she had sometimes accepted half-vocations, because she feared they would afterward be lost in the world, but that afterward they could be formed and then became true vocations, since, she added to me: «It is very hard to find vocations already formed and complete». Of only one she said to me: «This one was born with the veil».

One of the most important duties of her office being that of visiting the Houses of the Institute, she never neglected it, however much it cost her because of her habitual and sometimes extraordinary infirmities, and she attended to it to the last, though almost broken in health.

Once, going to meet her at the Palermo station, I

p. 431

XXXI witness (IV ex off.), Mrs. E. Settimo Princ. of Fitalia 431 saw her overwhelmed by headache, and I noticed on her forehead the protuberance, like a round head, not flat, of a nail, and asking her what she had on her forehead, she answered me: «It is the headache that makes me so».

Once I accompanied her on her visit to Monreale, and noticed that she brought joy and encouragement and contentment with her; it was Paradise that she brought to her Sisters.

In her decisions and in the choice of personnel she prayed, as I suppose, because she prayed over everything before deciding. I never heard that she let herself be guided by partiality or ulterior motives in her choices and decisions; but she directed herself in everything according to the will of God and the good of the Institute. From her talk I sometimes could understand that in some decision she had had to accommodate herself as best she could because of pressures put on her by persons of authority, from whom she could not withdraw.

§ 660
Development of the Institute.

Ad 23: The rapid development of the Institute from the earliest times must be attributed, in my opinion, to the blessing of God and the protection of St. Anne.

The Servant of God was so full of charity toward the others that I cannot even remotely think that she would ever have accepted from the local Superiors for the Generalate House anything more than the superfluous.

I have noticed in many Superiors a surge of great love toward the Servant of God, so that it may be that they made, and made their subjects make, some sacrifice to send something more to the Generalate House.

From what I heard, and from the way she treated her Sisters, one could see that the Servant of God was much occupied and concerned about the good treatment of her Daughters, and for this she had even fixed the menus for the Feasts, so that they might be well treated and at table too there might be a little feast.

I heard it told that the Servant of God very often went down herself to the kitchen to make sure with her own eyes how her Sisters were treated at table, and I heard it said that in the first times she helped to do the cooking.

Needless to say how much care she took of her sick Sisters. They were her passion, and sometimes she even helped them miraculously. She went personally to the infirmary, and tended them herself with limitless charity.

§ 661
Maternal concern for her son Alessandro.

Ad 24: As to relations with her family, I remember having observed a very great affection of her son toward her. Alessandro, for such was his name, ran after her even from afar. He sometimes came also to Sicily, when the Mother was there, and I observed that the Mother treated him with great coldness and tried to send him away. To my remarks that that son had come from so far, she answered: «No, no, this may not please the Sisters: it is better that he go away».

The son Alessandro went for some time to America, and there it seems he was in danger of sin; and the Servant of God, who learned it in a supernatural way, as I understood, felt such pain that, as she told me, she prayed the Lord so much that he not be made to offend him, and rather that he make him die, promising him that for this she would not shed a tear. Her son returned from America, radiant with youth and beauty, but a short time afterward he fell ill with consumption. His mother assisted him and nursed him at Piacenza; her son could no longer rise from his bed, he was reduced to a skeleton, and suffered so much from his gangrenous throat that it was often necessary to resort to morphine to give him a little respite. While the Mother was in this martyrdom she had the sweetest, most comforting words, and of greatest concern for me, answering almost daily with letters and telegrams, because I too was in tribulation over a rather serious illness of my husband, who was afterward miraculously cured by her, as I shall say in its place. Her son Alessandro died assisted by the Mother, although she did not at all neglect the affairs of the Institute. Her son being dead, she returned to her House to hear Mass there and make Holy Communion. The visit of the Bishop was then announced to her, that same morning; he stayed with her in totally indifferent conversation, as if her son had not died, and the Mother herself answered him with apparent indifference, but she suffered so much that afterward, telling it, she said to me: «Not even if a dog had died», and in these words her face expressed an indescribable sorrow.

p. 433

XXXI witness (IV ex off.), Mrs. E. Settimo Princ. of Fitalia 433

§ 662
Her family, a source of much suffering for the Servant of God.

As to her daughter and the latter's family, I shall say that they were the instrument of many sorrows and continual torments for her, as I perceived. And sometimes, seeing from some word that her son-in-law Gaspare Barbiellini made her suffer greatly, I said to her: «But Gaspare will surely be converted in the end, will he not?». She answered me once: «He will always remain an enemy of the Institute». Gaspare was not content to apply pressure personally himself, but pushed his little children, with blows, to wrest from their grandmother what she could not give.

Proc. fol. 2711: It is understood that, when I gave the Servant of God that money as a gift, I did not say that it was to give to her family, because it would have seemed to me an offense.

§ 663
Relations of the Servant of God with her relatives.

The Servant of God, as she told me, would have greatly wished that her daughter Carlotta, who was deaf-mute, become a religious rather than marry, and from childhood tried to direct her toward the religious life, but all was useless, and then she resigned herself to her marriage. I believe the late Princess Altieri was the one who offered to present Carlotta in society, and she then met Count Gaspare Barbiellini, who became her husband.

The Servant of God had to suffer also because of her daughter's love, who was extremely jealous of the Sisters, as has been told me by several Sisters. She was a good instrument for the self-interested aims of Gaspare, who launched her to the assault on the Mother, as also the children.

The Servant of God's favorite was the granddaughter Maria, but she too was a first-rate ingrate, and she too lent herself to her father's aims. All these things I heard said by Sisters. These relatives came, one may say, almost every day to the Servant of God. The Servant of God was vexed with them, as I could understand from the Sisters, and by the great sorrows they continually caused her. I know from the Sisters, and it seems also from the Servant of God, that Count Gaspare held the administration of the Gargatano for a certain time, but that afterward, she not being satisfied, she dismissed him and had him replaced. The Servant of God made use for a short time, for small affairs, also of Count Edoardo, Gaspare's brother, but, dissatisfied with him too, she dismissed him.

The Servant of God also had two brothers, Federico and Francesco, most devoted to her. Since Federico was a republican and also anticlerical, the Servant of God suffered immensely from it and was very serious, reserved, and I would even say cold with him, as I myself saw. He nevertheless lent himself to the Institute and greatly helped his sister with the building of this House, and helped the Sisters as much as he could. Francesco too lent himself to his sister's Institute, and after the death of the Servant of God both continued to lend themselves with affection. From the way the Servant of God spoke to me of Federico, I understood that she suffered greatly, and I therefore imagined that she did everything possible for his conversion. I myself said to the Servant of God, to comfort her: «But do not fear for Federico, because it is impossible that a brother of yours be lost». She then fell silent.

§ 664
Apostolic Visitation: attitude of the Servant of God toward the Visitor.

Ad 25: I know of the Apostolic Visitation made to the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, and it is my conviction that it came about through the machinations of Count Gaspare Barbiellini. I had to notice personally that Gaspare had it in for the Servant of God. She suffered greatly from this Apostolic Visitation, without showing it: appearing completely tranquil. And it is my conviction that this sorrow killed her, above all because of the idea that this measure came from the Holy See. Of her great sorrow I could become aware from her letters and her words. She added to me, however, by word of mouth, that she would be very happy to yield her place. This she repeated to me many times.

I have heard from Sisters that the Servant of God treated the Apostolic Visitor, Monsignor Serafini, now Cardinal, with great deference and veneration. As far as I know from the same Sisters, the Servant of God concealed nothing from him and was glad that he should see everything. She herself wrote to me that she had immediately given the Visitor the keys of everything at Piacenza, but that he refused them. She also told me that the Visitation would end in a triumph for the Institute.

Ad 26: The Servant of God, it is my conviction, always observed in the most perfect manner, even in the smallest things, the commandments of God, of the Church, and the obligations of her state, and procured, as far as lay in her, that they be observed also by others.

Ad 27: The Servant of God possessed and exercised all the Theological and Cardinal virtues and those connected with them.

p. 435

XXXI witness (IV ex off.), Mrs. E. Settimo Princ. of Fitalia 435

§ 665
Faith and life of continual prayer.

And, to begin with Faith, I shall say that in her there was that faith which moves mountains, and she communicated it to others. Her charity toward her neighbor was such, as I say, that she offered herself to God for others. How can one therefore think that she was not ready to suffer even martyrdom for God? From when she was in the world, she gave talks to the Daughters of Mary and then as a Religious also to her Sisters and Novices. She expressed to me, with great satisfaction, that her Sisters were in Africa and in America and that there they had children to educate, and she also expressed to me the desire that her Daughters be throughout the whole world to evangelize. From her conversation I understood that she also prayed for the conversion of sinners.

Her life was a continual prayer, day and night. Even when she spoke with me, I often noticed that her soul was completely and always united to God.

When she prayed in Church or in the Chapel I always saw her kneeling on the ground with a chair in front of her. She recommended prayer to all, and with me she insisted on meditation.

Proc. fol. 2719: The Servant of God did not write a letter without

§ 666
Devotion to Jesus Crucified. Other devotions.

mentioning the Crucifix, or closing it with him. In every conversation with me she made her Crucifix enter. The Crucifix was her life. In Holy Week one may say she was no longer of this earth: on Good Friday she shut herself in her room and no one saw her. Once at Palermo, being there in Holy Week, from Thursday, after the service, until Holy Saturday morning, I could not see her.

On the occasion of the twenty-fifth anniversary of the Institute, in which the Rules were also approved, I too brought my gift to the Servant of God, consisting of a gilded silver reliquary procured for me by certain Nuns. In this reliquary there is a small hand holding a long thorn. When I presented it to the Servant of God, my husband and I noticed an extraordinary expression of love in her gaze at that thorn: it seemed she had forgotten all those who surrounded her.

She nourished a devotion, love and filial trust toward Our Lady that were altogether extraordinary, as I saw from her talk and her writings.

While this Church was being built, the Servant of God, through Sr. A. del Salvatore, had me asked to make the Grotto of Our Lady of Lourdes in it at my expense, and I, together with my sister-in-law Felice Settimo di Fitalia, gave the necessary money and had a statue of Our Lady of Lourdes brought from Paris. The Servant of God wished it to be crowned, but Cardinal Verga objected that, being of carton-pierre, it could not be crowned, but he himself undertook to have one made of marble, and it was made with various contributions and so it was crowned with a golden crown, the Mother inviting us to contribute, there being nothing else fitting for Our Lady but gold and fine stones or pearls. To this Grotto many came to pray, and received many graces, so that a bulletin was drawn up which came out from time to time.

Afterward came her most tender devotion to St. Anne, and I would almost say that she was identified with this Saint.

St. Michael the Archangel she called in her letters «My Angel». Of St. Francis of Paola, to whom she also had a special devotion, I recall that the Servant of God made me understand that on the occasion of some persecution, I no longer remember which, the said Saint assured her that he would strike the persecutor with his staff.

§ 667
Very devoted to the Holy See and to the Holy Father.

She was also extraordinarily devoted to the Holy See: every order or wish that came from there was for her divine law, and for this her suffering over the Apostolic Visitation was the greater, and she inculcated it on me too. Needless to say how great was her devotion in a particular way to Pio Nono, who was for her like a Saint in Heaven; he was her protector, her Director, and everything; and Pio Nono had great affection for her. She told me that once, going to an audience, other persons being present, Pio Nono addressed himself at once to her, who had placed herself in a corner behind the others. Telling me this, she also told me of the great confusion she felt then, and of the immense condescension Pio Nono showed her. Pio Nono, jokingly, called her his ragamuffin. She also told me that, being, I believe, at Foligno when Pio Nono died, she saw a globe of fire rise to Heaven, and understood at once what it was about and exclaimed: «Ah, Pio Nono is dead», feeling great sorrow. She also urged me to give the Holy Father my mite.

Although she had to suffer from various Bishops, she never failed in her devotion also toward them.

p. 437

XXXI witness (IV ex off.), Mrs. E. Settimo Princ. of Fitalia 437

§ 668
Hope: her gaze always turned to heaven.

As to Hope, I shall say that her gaze was always turned to Heaven, and on the occasion of some tribulation of mine she exhorted me to bear it in peace, pointing me to Paradise.

Once I found the Servant of God greatly afflicted, and learned from herself that the Lord had let her know that Sr. A. Celsa Speranza was to die: she, however, then prayed so much that, doing violence to the Lord, she obtained that she should live.

Of the things of this world she cared nothing at all, whether honors or riches. In adversities, in contradictions, her only support was the thought of God; but the tribulations themselves were her comfort, and she told me that without tribulations she could not live; and she had them all her life. And I never saw her waver in her purposes, in her works, and yield for a single moment to mistrust. The greater the tribulation, the more her trust grew. To comfort me on the occasion of some sorrow, she wrote to me that after the tribulation fair weather would always come.

I have heard from Sisters that sometimes the money had grown in her hands up to what was needed in some circumstance: so great was her trust in the Lord!

And so much trust and so much hope was certainly not based on her merits, for she thought so little of herself that, speaking or writing to me, she called herself by the most contemptuous names, and even called herself «a monster of iniquity»! And from the way she spoke, one could well see that she said it with deep conviction, so that I suffered not a little. And while she so loved tribulation, she could not bear to see anyone suffer; and she desired the sufferings of others for herself in order to relieve them. To the poor, to the afflicted she instilled trust, besides with words, with the other means that were at her disposal.

In the Servant of God I never noticed even the smallest imperfection.

§ 669
Charity toward the poor and the sick.

Proc. fol. 2727v.: Charity toward neighbor. The Servant of God did what she could to help the poor, and with great zeal recommended it, because, she said, almsgiving wipes out sins: and she also asked her acquaintances for help for this or that family, and asked not only for extraordinary alms, but also for monthly contributions. She had bread, and also leftovers of food, given to the poor from the Generalate House.

Her charity toward the sick was extraordinary. Once she said to me: «In Paradise, where many daughters of St. Anne are already ranged, and I saw that St. Anne presented them to the Most Holy Trinity, the Teachers have their reward, but they, who think themselves something, are surpassed by the nurses, who have in addition a sash across the shoulder». She herself told me that her passion was the sick, because in them we must see our Lord. I have heard from several Sisters that she miraculously healed several sick Sisters.

§ 670
Particular charity toward persons opposed to her.

I understood from her talk, besides knowing it from other Sisters, that certain persons whom she knew to be opposed to her she treated with great amiability; and I asked myself: «How does the Mother manage to have all this amiability?», while, as I have heard the Sisters say, she showed in their faults and defects such severity of aspect that it inspired great fear, and it seemed to them they saw God himself angry.

Her bearing was then always such that it won hearts, so that those persons who came closest to her were ready for any sacrifice to please her and to spare her displeasure.

§ 671
Prudence: she did nothing without asking advice.

Prudence: She said to me: «One must never do anything without asking advice», and added that I should ask advice also of several persons. As to her spiritual direction, once she said to me: «The Lord has given to all, even to the Saints, a guide (and she cited St. Teresa) and to me the Lord has not granted so much grace; but now I confess to the Father General of the Minors, and I receive so much consolation, because he understands me completely». A year later she added to me again: «The Lord now permits that he no longer understand me; and it is a very painful trial!». Now I recall that she said that, besides asking advice, one must pray.

She gave me counsels with such humility that I had to ask her for them; the results were then such as to persuade me that she was enlightened from above.

I always saw her so busy that I sometimes had scruples about stealing a little of her time, although my soul from her

p. 439

XXXI witness (IV ex off.), Mrs. E. Settimo Princ. of Fitalia 439 received so much benefit and felt so great a need of it. She was, one may say, crushed by work; but in all this business I saw well that her union with God never ceased. I believe she dispatched her correspondence largely at night, as I know from herself.

As to Justice, I have a vague idea that the Servant of God recommended me to be very careful to pay the workmen justly.

§ 672
Gratitude.

Her gratitude toward me confounded and humbled me, while I felt myself a very great debtor toward her. And not only toward me, but toward any person who had done her the least good she showed herself most grateful. And this I understood from her talk.

As to temperance, I shall say that she was most mortified.

§ 673
Spirit of mortification.

Once, when the Institute was still in the Briuccia house, the Servant of God having to come to Palermo, and I knowing that because of excessive work she suffered in her eyes at night from the light of the petroleum, I sent to the house for her an oil lamp with a large flask of oil to burn, which was old, greenish, etc. Going afterward to their House after several days, meeting the Provincial Sr. Battistina Bertuzzi on the stairs, I asked her whether she had received the oil for the lamp and how it was going. She answered me in surprise: «But what oil?». «The one I sent for the lamp». «What do you mean, for the lamp? But that oil, after it arrived here, I have always used for the Mother, for her food». At this discovery we were left desolate and filled with admiration, because the Servant of God had eaten it as if it were nothing, and without even saying a word.

§ 674
Evangelical poverty.

Out of a spirit of poverty I know that she had one width of cloth less than the other Sisters in her habit, and I noticed sometimes that her habit was torn under the armpits, and I noted that her shoes were sometimes broken and worn. Her room here in Rome was furnished most modestly; there was a small iron bed with a mattress of leaves, without a mattress proper, without sheets; two or three rush-seated chairs, a rush-seated kneeler, an ordinary table, another table with a large Crucifix, everything most ordinary; on the Crucifix there was a pair of spectacles belonging to a certain Priest Professor, who was almost about to go blind, and who, miraculously cured by the Servant of God, left them on that Crucifix. This I heard told by the Sisters. I never asked the Mother for information about this, because, in spite of our great mutual affection, she overawed me at certain moments.

For example, toward the last times, while I was sitting beside her in her study, putting a hand on my knees she said to me: «Emilia, I have prayed to Jesus for you, and nothing will happen to you». I understood that it was for the future, because at that time I had nothing to fear; but I did not dare ask her anything, not even for my sister, whom I too would have wished to be included in this assurance of immunity. And neither afterward did I ever ask her for an explanation, although I desired it. I recall that at those words I felt within me a sure tranquility.

Many times the Servant of God told me that she slept very little.

She had at Piacenza a most private room, reached by a very narrow little stair, and into which no one ever entered during her life. In front of the door the Servant of God kept a screen, because she feared being spied on. Once, when I was at Piacenza, she promised me that late at night she would introduce me into her secret cell. I was happy at this promise, but waited in vain. The next day she said to me: «I did not come to fetch you, having reflected that another might hear and be jealous».

That cell of hers I saw only after her death, going to Piacenza from Milan expressly for this.

§ 675
Instruments of penance.

There was an iron bed, the most miserable imaginable, with a pillow without a case, on which a very thick iron chain was sewn all around, covering it entirely. There was also a great wooden Cross, taller than a person. On the arms of the Cross there were two pieces of iron to support the wrists. Hanging from one arm was a rosary of large wooden beads. On the floor there was another great Cross, on which it was supposed that the Mother slept.

§ 676
Fortitude: never overcome by adversity.

Proc. fol. 2737v.: The Servant of God was the valiant woman of the Gospel. She was never overcome either by adversity or by illness, nor discouraged. She herself told me that for her suffering was a delight.

In the beginnings of the Institute particularly, as M.

p. 441

XXXI witness (IV ex off.), Mrs. E. Settimo Princ. of Fitalia 441 Carrega told me, the poverty was extreme, and the oppositions and adversities many; but nothing prevailed against her strong spirit.

Sr. Maria Teresa Sorrentino, when she was in the world, herself thought of becoming Foundress of an Institute, on the suggestions of Cardinal Guarino. The Servant of God liked this young woman very much, and wanted her in her Institute, and one day she said to me, concerning Maria Teresa's project of foundation: «To found an Institute one needs a breast of bronze».

When she felt me downcast, she encouraged me, as she encouraged everyone.

It is difficult to explain how much she loved the beautiful virtue, but it was seen and understood from the whole of her.

§ 677
Obedience and submission to the authorities.

Of her obedience I can say that it was manifested above all on the occasion of the Apostolic Visitation.

Among the trials of the Servant of God there was also the one she had from the Cardinal Protector Verga, who was seized by a certain fondness for a certain Sr. Francesca who was assigned to the General Secretariat. The Cardinal was at first of great zeal and austerity and devotion toward the Institute and the Foundress in particular, and obtained for the Institute great advantages, chief among them the approval of the Rules. These antecedents made his change all the more painful to the Servant of God. He often sent plants to Sr. Francesca, and this mutual correspondence was noticed by the Sisters.

Once, when the Servant of God was going to Naples with Sr. Francesca, he proposed to accompany her, and did accompany her. One can imagine how much the Servant of God suffered! And then she wrote to me, so that, not knowing how to get out of this painful position, I might have her summoned to Rome through the Ministry; and I obtained it for her from the Minister, the Honorable Armò Palermitano, to whom, however, I did not tell the true reason. The Servant of God, in that letter she wrote me, spoke only in general of an embarrassment from which she wanted to escape, and also to see me in Rome. The Servant of God afterward sent Sr. Francesca to Naples and then the Cardinal's visits gradually became rarer, and Sr. Francesca ended by leaving the Institute and marrying.

§ 678
Humility.

I have already said something of her humility, in that she called herself a monster of iniquity. I shall add that she called herself an ass, a nefarious sinner, and similar expressions, and with such an accent that one could not in the least doubt her persuasion, and one had to think that she had such lights on the divine holiness as to oblige her intellect to reveal itself to her with horror.

By surprise I sometimes managed to kiss her hand, for otherwise she would not have allowed it. If I learned anything from her that could make her grow in my esteem, she did not tell it to me out of self-love, but only to do good to my soul, and moreover only with brief and fleeting hints.

In all the virtues of which I have spoken, the Servant of God not only persevered to the end, but always went on growing and perfecting herself in them, as I could discern every time I saw her.

§ 679
She touched the summit of holiness, on a par with the great saints.

Ad 28: It is my conviction that the Servant of God was not only a Saint, but touched the summit of holiness on a par with the

great Saints, such as St. Teresa, etc.

Virtue she practiced in the most heroic, simplest and most natural manner.

Ad 29: Her penances never prevented her from applying herself with perfection to her office as General, and I do not know that she ever exceeded in the exercise of the virtues, but I noted in her a perfect balance in all things.

§ 680
Relations of the witness with the Servant of God and the Institute.

Ad 30, Proc. fol. 2747: In the last years of her life the Servant of God once came to bid farewell to me and my husband at the Rome station, as we were leaving for Naples. When we had got into the carriage, many people entered our compartment with many suitcases. The Servant of God, who knew how much such confusion annoyed me, and not being alone, said: «Oh, how sorry I am that you will be uncomfortable!». We took leave, on my part with much emotion, and as soon as the Servant of God had gone out, to my surprise and my husband's, who attributed the fact to a prayer of the Servant of God, we suddenly saw all those people with their suitcases get off in great haste from our compartment, and we remained alone. For this and for other facts which I do not now recall, the Servant of God obtained graces even without necessity. I did not set out on a journey without first consulting the Servant of God; and my journeys, always directed by her, always turned out well. Among the letters handed over there is one in which she told me: «This year do not go to Poland, because you would have

p. 443

XXXI witness (IV ex off.), Mrs. E. Settimo Princ. of Fitalia 443 troubles. Go rather to your sister-in-law in the Pyrenees, where you will have a pleasant stay»; and so it was. Another time she wrote me to go to Poland after all, where we would have a pleasant stay, and so it was.

Another time she advised me against the building of a house of ours, and then advised it, and all went well.

The Servant of God told me that the benefactors of the Institute had the right, as St. Francis of Paola granted it to his own, to eat freely with her Sisters, and so she made me understand that I too would have this right in the House of Via d'Ossuna in Palermo. Because of these words of the Servant of God, having once gone up to the house of Via d'Ossuna, without asking I was about to enter the refectory, not to eat with the Sisters, but to see them. The Superior Sr. A. Maria Teresa Sorrentino, who is very attached to the Rules, with somewhat serious manners prevented me from entering. I felt hurt by this, did not let the Superior see it, but went away disturbed, remaining so the whole day. A couple of days later, that is, after the time necessary for the mail to arrive from Rome to Palermo, behold a letter from the Servant of God (which is among those handed over) in which she told me that she saw me disturbed and sad, and alluded clearly to the incident that had happened before.

Several other times, without my having written or said it to her, she wrote me that she saw me sad, that I should have courage, that I should be calm because such and such a thing would not happen.

§ 681
Favors attributed to the Servant of God during her life.

Ad 31, Proc. fol. 2748v.: Among the various facts I shall cite some. The first happened to myself. I suffered from a kind of catarrh in the nose; a humor prevented my breathing for many months, it seems to me more than a year; I suffered sleeping, I suffered awake, obliged to keep my mouth open to breathe. The nose was swollen, and when I blew it blood came out and also matter. I was much tormented: I had taken iodine baths at Ostia on the advice of a famous doctor of Warsaw. Although a little improved, I returned to the former state. Passing through Rome I spoke of it to the Servant of God, who, taking a reliquary out of her pocket, made a sign of the cross on my nose and said: «I do not want anything to come to your nose». I felt at once that the swelling had disappeared, and, back at the hotel, I asked my husband: «How does my nose look to you?». He, looking at me, answered: «Why, it seems to me you have nothing any more». I went into the other room and put the same question to my maid, Amelia Pieri, now deceased, who had been with me for many years, and she answered me: «It seems to me you have nothing». I then told the fact, and both were amazed. Many years have now passed, and I am very well.

The second grace was granted to the Prince, my husband. He suffered from an acute laryngitis. The vocal cords were affected, and he spoke with a thread of voice. My anguish was all the greater because the Prince did not take care of himself at all. I had several doctors come: Dr. Berlin, Professor Luzzatti of the University of Palermo, Dr. Filippo Maggiore (given name) Perni and others. With their questions they frightened me. They recommended that the patient not speak: they prescribed various cures, but no improvement came of them. According to my habit, I confided almost daily to the venerated Mother my anxieties, and she, although then occupied in caring for her son Alessandro at Piacenza, mortally ill of the trachea, did not cease to reassure me with letters and telegrams, and encouraged me with an unequalled charity to hope in God. I finally obtained from my husband to leave after Easter of the year 1891 for Naples to consult Professor Massei, to whose consultation the Mother urged me. He encouraged us to hope, assuring us that the Prince would recover from the laryngitis. He wished, however, to examine the chest, and found the sound on the right side much duller than on the left. I myself, from the place where I was sitting, could hear the difference in the sound given out under the tap of the Doctor's fingers: I was left most distressed, but the thought that we were going to see the venerated Mother sustained me. Arrived in Rome, I ran to the Servant of God: I told her what Dr. Massei had found, but she said to me: «Be calm, do not fear», and reassured me. I spent as usual hours of paradise with her and, according to custom, she had us lunch the next day in the guest quarters of the Convent, and was present at our lunch, during which she took the marsala that was prepared on the table and poured some with her own hands into my husband's little glass, and he drank it. Knowing the holiness of these blessed hands, I felt great consolation, knowing how many graces others had obtained by drinking a few drops of water or wine given by the Servant of God. And I was not mistaken. Having to leave the next day, we stayed

p. 445

XXXI witness (IV ex off.), Mrs. E. Settimo Princ. of Fitalia 445 a little longer after lunch. And remaining alone with the venerated Mother, she said to me: «When you arrive in Naples, go to Professor Massei; have the Prince examined again and you will see that he will find nothing more». And so it was in fact. The Professor, after listening to the chest, assured us with surprise that there was nothing more, and I too ascertained that its sound was clear, as on the other side. In my joy I did not think of having the Professor make out a certificate, and I regret it very much.

I must add further that Professor Luzzatti would have wished to give my husband Koch injections, to verify whether it was a case of consumption; I wrote to the Servant of God for advice, and she answered me: «I forbid you to do it».

§ 682
Recollections of the book «Consolations and Labors, etc.».

Ad 32, Proc. fol. 2766: The Servant of God published a book with a title given her by Cardinal Guarino, and which I think is the following: «Consolations and Labors, etc.». It consisted entirely of allegories and symbols, which referred to the history of the Institute and to her own, because connected with its foundation.

The first approval she had from Gonfalonieri, Canon Reviser Theologian of the Florentine Curia, and his letter of approval must still exist.

The second she had from Cardinal Guarino, and a third from Canon Pennino, Reviser of the Curia of Palermo. I had it printed, after that of Confalonieri, at Palermo, in two or three parts, with the permission of the local Curia. Then I had it reprinted with a preface composed of extracts from two letters of approval, from Canon Pennino and from Cardinal Guarino, very highly regarded in mystical matters. I believe that the enemies of the Servant of God made use of the first edition to create troubles for her. This book was afterward prohibited by the Superiors, and I know that the Servant of God hastened to write to Sr. Maria Teresa Sorrentino that all the copies be withdrawn at once. The Servant of God said to me, I think after the prohibition, as she had also said to me before: «This book will one day be read with fruit, because it is not I who wrote it». And one could understand that it was Our Lord who had dictated it to her.

Some time after the prohibition, I went to Fr. Lepidi, Master of the Sacred Palace, saying to him: «How is it that this book, which has done so much good to my soul, must be withdrawn from circulation?». And he answered me: «The sun too does so much good, but not everyone can bear it. Even to certain Sisters, not sufficiently balanced, it might do harm, because they might not understand it».

The Servant of God never let me know that she had been grieved by the said prohibition. She also said: «That book is Jesus's and Jesus will see to it».

Ad 33: I saw the Servant of God again in the autumn of 1899, and found her suffering greatly. But I hoped she would not die. On this occasion she told me that the Institute was well founded and consolidated, that even a little girl could govern it; a concept which I afterward learned she repeated to the Cardinal Protector Rampolla. I still keep a few lines of hers written to me a few days before her death.

On that last occasion when I saw her again, she hinted to me, in a way I no longer remember well, St. Anne's desire that her daughters be established also in Poland, and «oh! how many beautiful vocations I see in that country» she added.

Ad 37: Every year, passing through Rome, I always go to the tomb of the Servant of God, I feel great comfort, and have Masses said.

§ 683
Reputation for holiness in life and after death.

Ad 38: During her life, the Servant of God was held among the Sisters and among outsiders who had known her in the repute of a Saint. I know of various persons who came to commend themselves to her prayers, Signora Frascara, now deceased, Princess Lanza di Belmonte, and others. After her death, the same esteem as a saint has lasted among the Sisters, and I believe also among outsiders, but I have no precise recollections.

Ad 40: I, who commend myself to the Servant of God in every circumstance, small and great, of my life, continually experience her patronage and count on it, she having explicitly promised me to help me always. This is my great comfort in all the contingencies of my life, everything is lightened for me, it gives me trust and support.

I no longer remember in particular graces and miracles worked by the Servant of God after her death, in favor of her Sisters and of outsiders; many have been told me, and now I no longer remember them.

p. 447

XXXII witness (V ex off.), Sr. Anna Serafina Gregori 447

If I had noted everything down I would have had another great quantity of things to say, which now I am sorry no longer to remember.
